items.title: Native-speaker bus v0 — Meraki ↔ Z (direct-session pilot)
items.body:
# Native-speaker bus v0 — direct sessions, shared record

**Purpose.** Pilot a simple shared bus for **native Meraki (ChatGPT) ↔ native Z (Mistral/Vibe)**, with Mark as human owner. This is **not** the Allur OpenRouter proxy runner: **no new provider calls, no automated agent invocation, and no modeled stand-in for either native session.**

## The place
- **This GitHub issue is the bus.** Each new comment is an append-style message. GitHub supplies server timestamps, comment IDs, and an inspectable history. Do not rewrite earlier comments to change the record; publish a CORRECTION comment instead. GitHub issue comments are editable/deletable by authorized users, so this is an *auditable collaboration log*, **not** immutable/tamper-proof storage.
- **The ledger lives in the same thread initially** as explicitly marked OBSERVATION, QUESTION, DECISION, CORRECTION, or STOP comments; dialogue messages are marked MESSAGE. Later we can generate a JSONL export and a curated scientific ledger with provenance, if this manual pilot warrants it.
- **Two different native chat sessions must actually participate.** A native session reads the latest issue/comments via its own available tools and posts its own labeled comment. A post relayed by Mark must be marked `transport: Mark relay` rather than presented as direct tool access.
- No continuous link, background watcher, shared internal state, or guaranteed notifications exists. A model receives nothing until its session is prompted to read the issue; posting here does **not** notify the other model inside its chat.

## Pilot message header
```text
BUS v0
seat: Meraki | Z | Mark
kind: MESSAGE | OBSERVATION | QUESTION | DECISION | CORRECTION | ERROR | STOP
transport: native GitHub connector | Mark relay
reply_to: <comment ID or none>
text:
<one substantive message>
```
The GitHub comment ID and `created_at` timestamp, not a model's guessed sequence number or local clock, establish the canonical order. The visible seat label is an attribution claim; it is not cryptographic identity proof. If two messages cross, preserve both and reply by comment ID. Natural conversational flow beats forced round-robin; explicit floor handoff can be used when useful.

## Boundaries
1. **Public repository and public issue**: share only material Mark intends to publish. No protected/private notebooks, API keys, personal records, unapproved transcripts, or employer/client details.
2. No model API spend and no automation in v0. Any later live runner, polling, bridge, or publication/export is a separately approved change.
3. Only Mark authorizes scope, publication, and acceptance. Meraki and Z can contribute and challenge each other without fabricating consent, continuity, experiments, or platform telemetry.
4. A failed read/write is recorded as an ERROR with the source and plain failure summary; do not impersonate a successful handoff.

## Pilot success criterion
(1) Meraki posts one native-session comment; (2) Z independently reads this thread and responds, ideally using his own connected GitHub tool; (3) Meraki reads Z's **actual** comment and replies; (4) each labels what was observed versus inferred. If Z lacks write access, Mark may ferry Z's exact text with an explicit relay label. No claim of direct tool connectivity in that case.

## Companion
The existing OpenRouter `island/runner.py` and `bus` branch remain untouched. This issue is an intentionally small, parallel native-speaker pilot.

items.title: [FEATURE] [RFC] Dynamic Semantic Tool Selection for ML Commons Agents
items.body:
## Summary

Agents in ML Commons expose their entire configured tool set to the LLM on every turn. As the tool catalog grows, this consumes an increasing share of the prompt and gives the model more opportunities to pick the wrong tool.

This RFC proposes **opt-in tool search** for agents with many tools:
- The LLM sees a small fixed set of **pinned** tools plus one extra tool, `search_tools`.
- When none of its visible tools fits, the agent calls `search_tools` with a short phrase.
- The best-matching tools (by embedding similarity) are **appended** to its tool list for the rest of the run.

The feature ships as **experimental**:
- It's off by default.
- It applies only to agents that opt in.
- When off, behaviour is identical to today.

> **Revision history**
>
> - **v1** chose a tool subset up front from the user's question (cosine + MMR). We implemented and measured it. It missed a needed tool in most questions, and a tool the model is never shown can't be used, so v2 replaced it with agent-driven tool search.
> - **v3 (this revision, after review)** changes four things:
>   - the embedding cache moves from a system index to a **node-local in-memory cache**;
>   - pinned tools and `top_k` become **per-agent** settings, with no default pinned list;
>   - a **`max_dynamic_tools`** cap is added;
>   - the feature is **experimental and per-agent opt-in**.
>
>   v3 also adds a second evaluation round (**two LLMs**, 22 questions, mean and total tokens alongside the median) and an **FAQ** answering review questions. Details: Evaluation §4, FAQ.
>
>   It also specifies behaviour settled while implementing and reviewing it:
>   - tools the model used earlier in a conversation stay visible on the next message;
>   - the cache embeds in chunks and expires entries after an hour;
>   - `tool_selection` can be changed with the existing update agent API.

---

## Problem statement

### Current behaviour

Tool descriptions are concatenated into the prompt for every agent turn:

- `AgentUtils.getToolsPromptMap` builds `${parameters.tool_descriptions}` from all tools.
- `MLChatAgentRunnerV2` calls `AgentUtils.addToolsToFunctionCalling(toolsMap, llmParams, toolNames, "")` with the full `toolsMap.keySet()`.

Every configured tool's name, description, and schema is present on every turn, regardless of what the user asked. Measured on a 33-tool agent, the tool definitions alone are about 5,100 tokens (roughly 220 per tool) on **every** LLM call.

### Why this matters more over time

1. **Catalogs grow.** `opensearch-mcp-server-py` ships 50+ tools across categories (core, observability, search relevance, agentic memory, skills). Only the `core_tools` category (9 tools) is enabled by default, but deployments that enable more categories, or connect several MCP servers, quickly reach dozens of tools.
2. **Generated tools add more.** The server can also generate tools from the OpenSearch API specification. Today that generator is limited to a handful of operations, but it's a growth path.
3. **The current workaround gives up schemas.** `GenericOpenSearchApiTool` ([opensearch-mcp-server-py#109](https://github.com/opensearch-project/opensearch-mcp-server-py/issues/109) → [PR #112](https://github.com/opensearch-project/opensearch-mcp-server-py/pull/112)) was introduced to "reduce tool explosion by providing a single interface for all OpenSearch APIs." It works, but it collapses many typed, schema-bearing tools into one untyped one. That trades away the schema information that makes tool calls reliable.

Configuration-time filtering (which tools an agent has) doesn't address this: it must be decided before the question is known.

---

## Proposal

### Architecture

```
                        user question
                              |
                              v
  +------------------------------------------------------------+
  |  EXISTING                                                  |
  |    AgentUtils.getMlToolSpecs()    <- inline agent tools    |
  |    AgentUtils.getMcpToolSpecs()   <- MCP-fetched tools     |
  |    AgentUtils.createTools()       <- effective name + desc |
  |    -> toolsMap: every tool the agent would expose          |
  +------------------------------------------------------------+
                              |
                              v
  +------------------------------------------------------------+
  |  DynamicToolSelector.plan()   (new, opt-in, no model call) |
  |    agent opted in? more than min_pool_size tools?          |
  |    -> prompt tools = the agent's pinned tools              |
  |                      + search_tools                        |
  |    -> background: warm the hidden tools' embeddings        |
  +------------------------------------------------------------+
                              |
                              v
  +------------------------------------------------------------+
  |  EXISTING ReAct loop (MLChatAgentRunnerV2)                  |
  |    LLM sees: pinned tools + search_tools (+ found tools)   |
  |                                                            |
  |    model calls search_tools("explain why shard is          |
  |                              unassigned allocation")       |
  |       1. embed the phrase                                  |
  |       2. cosine-rank the hidden tools (cached vectors)     |
  |       3. append the top_k to the prompt tool list          |
  |          (up to max_dynamic_tools in total)                |
  |       4. return "Found N tools: ..." as a tool result      |
  |                                                            |
  |    tool calls always execute against the full toolsMap     |
  +------------------------------------------------------------+
```

### Where the hook lives

Tool search applies inside the V2 agent runner, after `AgentUtils.createTools` has populated `toolsMap`, and before the first LLM call. It doesn't go inside `getMlToolSpecs`, for two reasons:

1. **`getMlToolSpecs` can't see MCP tools.** It returns only the agent's inline tools. `MLChatAgentRunnerV2` separately calls `getMcpToolSpecs` and appends the result. MCP tools are the main source of large catalogs, so hooking `getMlToolSpecs` would leave all of them in the prompt.
2. **Tool descriptions don't exist yet at that point.** `MLToolSpec.getDescription()` is frequently null. The description that reaches the prompt comes from the tool factory default and any per-agent override, both applied inside `AgentUtils.createTool`.

### How it works

**Pinned tools.** A per-agent list of tool names that are always visible, in configured order.
- Names an agent doesn't have are ignored.
- There's no default list.
- For agents built on `opensearch-mcp-server-py`, the recommended list is its `core_tools` set: `ListIndexTool`, `IndexMappingTool`, `SearchIndexTool`, `GetShardsTool`, `ClusterHealthTool`, `CountTool`, `ExplainTool`, `MsearchTool`, `GenericOpenSearchApiTool`.
- Pinning matters. `GenericOpenSearchApiTool` is the only route to several endpoints (snapshots, allocation explain), but its generic description matches no specific search.
- An agent with no pinned tools still works, but it searches more.

**`search_tools`.** An ordinary tool, created per run, with a `query` argument.
- Its description **names the hidden tools** (sorted, at most 100), so the model knows what it can ask for.
- In live testing, a description with only a count made the agent search far less often (see Evaluation).
- The description is fixed for the life of a run.

**Ranking.** The phrase is embedded with the configured `TEXT_EMBEDDING` model. Each hidden tool is scored by **exact cosine similarity** against its cached description embedding, and the top `top_k` (default 5) are returned.

Exact rather than k-NN: the pool is one agent's tools (tens to low hundreds), so scoring all of them:
- takes microseconds;
- never misses a match;
- needs no k-NN plugin or fixed vector dimension.

**Appending, not swapping.** Found tools are appended after the pinned prefix and stay for the rest of the run. Tools are never removed or reordered, so the start of the prompt (pinned tools + `search_tools`) is identical on every call. That keeps provider-side prompt caches valid (see Evaluation: caching).

**Bounded growth.** At most `max_dynamic_tools` found tools (default 15, three searches at `top_k` 5) are appended in a run. Once the cap is reached:
- `search_tools` returns "tool limit reached; continue with the tools you have" and adds nothing;
- it stays in the list, because removing it would change the prompt prefix.

**Execution is not filtered.** Tool calls run against the agent's full tool set. Hiding a tool shortens the prompt; it isn't an access control.
- A model can call a hidden tool directly by name, since `search_tools` lists the names. It then hasn't seen that tool's schema.
- When it does, the call runs, and the tool is appended to the visible list as if it had been found, so its schema is shown from the next call. It counts toward `max_dynamic_tools`.
- Observed in 1 of 195 tool-search runs.

**Tools used earlier in the conversation stay visible.** At the start of each run, configured tools that the conversation history already called are shown right after the pinned tools: most recent first, up to `max_dynamic_tools`.
- They're part of the run's fixed prefix and don't count toward the cap.
- The history's tool calls then always refer to tools in the request, and the model doesn't have to search again for a tool it already used.

**No cost until the agent searches.** Deciding whether tool search applies makes no model call. A run where the agent never searches makes no embedding call for the question at all.

### Configuration

Experimental, and off by default. At **cluster** level there are only the on/off switch, the embedding model and the search timeout:

```json
PUT /_cluster/settings
{
  "persistent": {
    "plugins.ml_commons.tool_selection.enabled": true,
    "plugins.ml_commons.tool_selection.embedding_model_id": "<model_id>"
  }
}
```

| Cluster setting | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `tool_selection.enabled` | `false` | Feature flag and kill switch. When `false`, no agent uses tool search. |
| `tool_selection.embedding_model_id` | `""` | Default `TEXT_EMBEDDING` model. Admin-only. Blank forces the feature off. |
| `tool_selection.search_timeout` | `5s` | Time budget per search. Admin-only. |

Everything about **which tools and how many** is per agent, and an agent uses tool search only if it opts in:

```json
POST /_plugins/_ml/agents/_register
{
  "name": "My Agent",
  "type": "conversational_v2",
  "tool_selection": {
    "enabled": true,
    "pinned_tools": ["ListIndexTool", "SearchIndexTool", "ClusterHealthTool", "GenericOpenSearchApiTool"],
    "top_k": 5,
    "max_dynamic_tools": 15
  },
  "tools": [ ... ]
}
```

| Agent field (`tool_selection`) | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `false` | Opt this agent in. |
| `pinned_tools` | `[]` | Always-visible tools. |
| `top_k` | `5` | Tools added per search. |
| `min_pool_size` | `10` | With this many tools or fewer, the agent sees all of them. |
| `max_dynamic_tools` | `15` | Cap on tools appended in one run. |
| `embedding_model_id` | cluster default | Per-agent model, for example under multi-tenancy, where a model belongs to one tenant. |

No new API. `tool_selection` is accepted by the existing register and update agent APIs.
- **Update:** an update changes only the fields it sets. A null isn't accepted in an update, because an update keeps every stored field it leaves out, so a null couldn't reset anything. To turn tool search off for an agent, set `enabled` to `false`.
- **Storage:** the field is omitted from stored documents when unset, so existing agents serialize exactly as before.
- **Mixed-version clusters:** it's sent between nodes only from the release that adds it, so they keep working.

### Embedding cache

- **What's cached:** a **node-local, bounded, in-memory cache** holds one vector per distinct tool description.
- **The key:** a SHA-256 over the embedding model id, the tenant id and the description, each length-prefixed so no field can run into the next.
  - A per-agent description override gets its own vector.
  - Tenants never share entries.
  - Two agents with the same description share one entry.
- **Nothing is persisted:** no system index, no mapping, and no remote-store or multi-tenancy storage question.
- **Size:** bounded by weight (50 MB by default), evicting least-recently-used entries. One vector is dimensions × 4 bytes, so 1,000 descriptions at 3,072 dimensions take about 12 MB.
- **Expiry:** an entry expires an hour after it's written. That bounds how long a vector can outlive a change the key can't see, such as the connector behind an embedding model id being switched.
- **Warm-up:** at the start of a run, the hidden tools' embeddings are warmed in the background, so the first search is usually a hit.
  - Misses are embedded in chunks of 32 descriptions, below common provider batch limits, and each chunk is cached as it completes.
  - A search that starts while warm-up is still running waits for that batch instead of embedding again, for at most 2 minutes.
- **When it re-embeds:** a node embeds a description once:
  - when it first runs an agent with that description;
  - again after a restart;
  - again if the description or the embedding model changes. The key changes then, so stale vectors are never used;
  - again an hour after the entry was written.

  A batch for a 30-tool agent is about 1,000–2,500 tokens, a fraction of a cent.
- **No persistence in v1.** A persistent store can be added later if it's ever needed (thousands of descriptions, short-lived nodes, or slow self-hosted embedding models).

### Failure behaviour

Tool search is an optimisation, and an optimisation that can fail a user's request is a bug.

- **Before the run, the agent sees every tool exactly as today if:**
  - the feature is off;
  - no model is configured;
  - the agent hasn't opted in;
  - the agent has `min_pool_size` tools or fewer;
  - every tool is pinned;
  - the agent already has a tool named `search_tools`.
- **During a search, every outcome reaches the model as an ordinary tool result:**
  - matches;
  - "no matching tools";
  - "all tools are already loaded";
  - "tool limit reached";
  - on timeout or embedding failure, "tool search is unavailable, continue with the tools you have".
- **The search timeout** is enforced with `ListenerTimeouts`, so a slow embedding model can never stall an agent.
- **Embedding errors are contained:**
  - a chunk that fails, or whose response doesn't carry exactly one vector per input, caches nothing;
  - a search ranks the tools that do have vectors, and reports "unavailable" only when none do;
  - vectors are never matched to the wrong tool.
- **Security context:** a run that waits on another run's in-flight batch continues under its own security context, not the other run's.

### Observability

- **Per execution:** one log line with `applied`, pool size, pinned tools and searchable count, or the skip reason.
- **Per search:** one log line with the tools found, latency, and any timeout or failure.
- **Per direct call to a hidden tool:** one log line.
- **Not logged:** the search phrase, because it's derived from user input.

---

## Evaluation

All measurements used the real `opensearch-mcp-server-py` catalog and realistic operator questions, each labelled with the tools genuinely needed.
- An independent second labeller produced a second answer key, and offline results are reported against both.
- Embeddings: Gemini `gemini-embedding-001`.
- The main offline metric is **"was every needed tool available to the model"**, all or nothing, because a single missing tool can silently break the answer.

### 1. Up-front selection (this RFC's first version) doesn't work

61 tools (53 MCP + 8 ml-commons), show 4:

| Ranking | Every needed tool kept |
|---|---|
| Cosine + MMR (lambda 0.5) | 19–25% |
| Plain cosine | 31–38% |
| Plain + Gemini task_type, or hybrid (0.7 vector + 0.3 BM25) | 38–44% |

MMR lost 16 of 16 head-to-head comparisons against plain ranking. Tool descriptions resemble each other (median cosine 0.64) more than any question (0.55), so the redundancy penalty outweighs relevance.

### 2. Agent-driven search does

Simulated agent search phrases, written by a labeller who never saw the tool list (2.8 per question), top 3 per search:

| Design | Every needed tool found | Tools shown |
|---|---|---|
| One search with the user's question | 31–44% | 3 |
| The agent's own phrases | 56–75% | ~7 |
| + 9 core tools pinned | **94% (both answer keys)** | ~15 of 61 |

The agent's own short phrases are much better queries than the user's question, and pinning is essential.

### 3. Live benchmark, round 1: 144 runs, one model

**Setup:**
- a `conversational_v2` agent (Claude Sonnet 4.5);
- the 33-tool MCP server (write tools off) and sample data;
- 16 questions × 3 repeats, with and without tool search;
- 8 questions graded automatically against live cluster facts.

**Results:**
- input tokens per LLM call fell from 7,731 to **3,173**;
- graded answers: 18/24 without tool search, **19/24** with it;
- median seconds per question rose from 7.7 to 10.7;
- search latency: 1.5 s median, 0 timeouts.

**Observations:**
- **Matched work was faster.** When both versions did the same work, tool search was 0.7 s faster, because the prompt is smaller.
- **Searches were accurate.** Every search phrase the agent wrote was on topic, and whenever a matching tool existed it came back in the top 5. For example, "explain why shard is unassigned allocation" returned `GetAllocationTool` in 6 of 6 runs.
- **Naming hidden tools matters.** Listing the hidden tools in `search_tools` more than doubled how often the agent searched (from earlier live runs).

### 4. Live benchmark, round 2: two models, search-path questions

Added after review:
- **Six new graded questions** (22 in total), each best answered by a tool that **isn't pinned**, so the search path is exercised.
- **A second LLM.**
- **Mean and total tokens** alongside the median.

Arms: **A** = all 33 tools; **B** = tool search (9 pinned tools + `search_tools`). 3 repeats each.

| | Claude A | Claude **B** | Gemini A | Gemini **B** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Graded answers correct | 32/41 (78%) | **35/42 (83%)** | 28/42 (67%) | **26/41 (63%)** |
| Correct when the agent searched | – | **14/14** | – | **9/14** |
| Input tokens / question, median | 15,258 | **8,034** | 2,798 | **1,182** |
| Input tokens / question, mean | 16,920 | **9,908** | 3,090 | **1,874** |
| **Total input tokens vs A** | 100% | **59%** | 100% | **61%** |
| Mean of per-question ratios vs A | – | 69% | – | 72% |
| Questions where B used more tokens than A | – | 3 of 22 | – | 2 of 22 |
| Seconds / question, median | 9.0 | 10.8 | 9.1 | 13.1 |
| Questions with a search | – | 35% | – | 33% |
| Search latency, median | – | 1.4 s | – | 2.6 s |
| Runs that hit the step limit | 3 | 6 | 2 | 0 |
| Labelled tools available | – | 64% | – | 60% |

Models: Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Gemini 2.5 Pro, both through an OpenAI-compatible gateway.

**What it shows:**

- **Token savings hold across both models.** Tool search used 59% (Claude) and 61% (Gemini) of the all-tools total.
  - The median (38% and 41%) looks better, because it hides a few investigation-heavy questions where tool search took extra steps.
  - At list price, Claude's cost per question fell from $0.056 to $0.037.
- **Accuracy is within noise on both models.**
  - Gemini's two-run gap is mostly one question, where one of the two misses was a grader wording miss.
  - On the search path, Claude answered 14/14.
  - Gemini answered 9/14. Three of its misses are a question Gemini also fails without tool search (0/3), so they come from the model, not the search.
- **Latency rises** by +1.8 s (Claude) and +4.0 s (Gemini) at the median: an extra model turn plus the embedding call. See Risks.
- **A search-before-asking prompt changes the trade-off.** A third Claude arm added a system prompt telling the agent to search before asking the user. It searched in 51% of questions and scored 85%, but used 85% of the all-tools tokens.
- **Absolute token counts aren't comparable across models.** Compare B with A within a model.

### 5. Prompt caching

Measured with the 33 real tool definitions, using the provider's cache usage figures:

- **Without cache markers there is no cache to lose.** Through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, identical requests showed 0 cached tokens.
- **With Anthropic `cache_control` markers, tool search is still cheaper.** The same 3-turn conversation cost $0.0446 with all tools and **$0.0198 with tool search (56% less)**.
- **Appending keeps most of the cache.** The turn on which 5 found tools were appended still read 63% of its prompt from cache, and the next turn read 99%.
- **The pinned prefix is shared.** A new conversation reused 88% of it.
- **Swapping tools does lose the cache.** A design that changes the tool subset per question (this RFC's first version) never hit the cache. Appending to a fixed pinned set avoids that.

### 6. What text to embed per tool

We compared embedding the description alone with variants adding the tool name and argument names/descriptions.
- On this catalog, adding them didn't change which tools were found.
- It slightly lowered ranking quality (MRR 0.929 vs 0.905).
- Description-only is kept.

### Limitations

- **Narrow setup:** one MCP server and a small synthetic cluster. Two LLMs, both reached through the same gateway.
- **Accuracy precision:** 14 graded search-path runs per model rule out a large accuracy drop, but can't measure a small one.
- **Agents search less than the simulation assumed.**
  - Live labelled-tool availability was 60–69%, against 94% simulated.
  - That's mostly the agent asking the user for details instead of investigating, which happens with or without tool search.

---

## Scope

### In scope for v1 (experimental)

- `search_tools`, per-agent pinned tools and `max_dynamic_tools` in the V2 agent runner (`conversational_v2`), after `createTools`, behind the settings above.
- A node-local in-memory embedding cache keyed by model, tenant and description, with background warm-up, chunked embedding and one-hour expiry.
- Tools called earlier in the conversation shown after the pinned tools.
- `tool_selection` on the register and update agent APIs.
- Exact cosine ranking (top `top_k`), a search timeout with fail-open, and `min_pool_size` for small agents.
- Appending a hidden tool that the model calls directly.
- Observability as above.
- Unit and integration tests, and docs marking the feature experimental.

### Agent types

- **`conversational_v2`:** this RFC.
- **Flow and conversational-flow agents:** not applicable. They run a fixed tool sequence, and the model never chooses tools.
- **V1 `conversational`:** a follow-up. Its tool list is built in a similar place.
- **`plan_execute_and_reflect`:** gets it through its executor agent (`executor_agent_id`) once V1 `conversational` has it.

### Follow-ups

- **Keep found-but-unused tools across messages.** Tools the model called carry over to the next message (see How it works). Tools that were found but never called don't, so a follow-up message may search for them again.
- **Hybrid ranking** (vector + BM25). It gave a small gain offline.
- **Agent Skills alignment (#4648).** Skills disclose *instructions* on demand, and tool search discloses *tool definitions* on demand. To avoid two mechanisms, a skill that declares the tools it needs could append them through the same append-only path, counted against the same `max_dynamic_tools` cap.
- **Provider prompt caching for agents:** `cache_control` / `cachePoint` markers, and an Anthropic Messages model provider. This lowers cost for every agent, and tool search keeps the prefix cache-friendly.

---

## Risks and trade-offs

- **Latency.** Each search is an extra model turn plus one embedding call.
  - Median time per question rose 20% (Claude) and 44% (Gemini) in round 2.
  - Mitigations: pinning the most-used tools keeps searches rare for common questions, and small agents skip the feature entirely.
- **More steps on some questions.**
  - Investigation-heavy questions can take more turns and use more tokens than sending everything (3 of 22 questions on Claude).
  - Claude hit the step limit in 6 runs with tool search versus 3 without.
  - The totals still favour tool search (59–61% of all-tools tokens), but per-question cost is more variable.
- **The agent may not search when it should.**
  - Live labelled-tool availability was 60–69%, mostly because models ask the user for details instead of investigating.
  - Naming the hidden tools in `search_tools` helps.
  - An agent system prompt such as "investigate with your tools before asking; if none fits, call search_tools" helps more (85% accuracy in round 2), at the cost of extra steps.
- **The benefit depends on the model.** Search-path accuracy was 14/14 on Claude and 9/14 on Gemini (where the misses weren't caused by search). Agents should be tested on their own model before relying on the feature, which is one reason it ships as experimental.
- **Search quality is capped by description quality.** If two tools have vague, near-identical descriptions, no embedding model will separate them. Better tool descriptions (the conclusion of #2151) remain a prerequisite.
- **Calling a hidden tool directly.** A model can call a hidden tool by name without having seen its schema. The call runs, and the tool is then appended so later calls see the schema. Seen in 1 of 195 tool-search runs.

---

## Alternatives considered

1. **Up-front selection from the user's question, with MMR** (this RFC's first version). Implemented and measured.
   - It kept every needed tool in only 19–44% of questions, and MMR made it worse.
   - Changing the tool subset per question defeats prompt caching.
   - Rejected.
2. **Improve tool descriptions instead** (the #2151 conclusion). Cheaper and effective for accuracy, and should happen anyway. It doesn't address prompt size. Complementary.
3. **Collapse tools into generic ones** (`GenericOpenSearchApiTool`). Already shipped, but trades away per-tool schemas. This proposal keeps typed tools, and pins the generic one as a fallback.
4. **Header-based filtering** ([opensearch-mcp-server-py#169](https://github.com/opensearch-project/opensearch-mcp-server-py/issues/169)). Solves permission scoping, but still requires deciding the set before the question is known.
5. **Static Toolkits** ([#1161](https://github.com/opensearch-project/ml-commons/issues/1161)). Requires an author to anticipate task shapes. Tool search is the dynamic form.
6. **A single `call_tool(name, args)` dispatcher** instead of appending found tools.
   - It never changes the tool list, so it's maximally cache-friendly.
   - But it loses the provider's schema validation for the real tool's arguments.
   - Appending keeps typed tools and, as measured, still keeps most of the cache.
7. **Provider-native tool search** (for example, Anthropic's tool search tool). It works the same way, but is provider-specific. ml-commons supports several providers, so it needs a provider-neutral version.
8. **A system index for the embedding cache** (this RFC's v2).
   - It survives restarts and is shared by all nodes.
   - But it needs `SdkClient` support (no multi-get or delete-by-query there), a mapping, and old-model cleanup, all for vectors that are cheap to recompute.
   - Replaced by the in-memory cache; persistence can be added later if it's ever needed.

---

## FAQ

**What if the agent needs a tool later in the task that the opening question didn't suggest?**
It searches at that point. Discovery happens inside the loop, not up front. For example, for "why is one of my shards unassigned?", the agent searched "explain why shard is unassigned allocation" and got `GetAllocationTool`, in 6 of 6 runs.

**Doesn't changing the tool list break prompt caching?**
Only swapping does. Found tools are appended after a fixed prefix (pinned tools + `search_tools`) and never removed or reordered, so the prefix stays cacheable.
- **Measured** (Evaluation §5): the turn that appended tools still read 63% from cache, and the next turn read 99%.
- **Cost:** with cache markers, tool search cost 56% less than all tools.

**How was recall evaluated?**
- **Labels:** each question is labelled with the tools genuinely needed, by two independent labellers.
- **Offline:** "every needed tool available" reached 94% with pinning.
- **Live:** labelled-tool availability was 60–69%, and end-task accuracy was graded against live cluster data on two models (Evaluation §3–4).

**Can I make sure some tools are always available?**
Yes. List them in the agent's `pinned_tools`. They're always visible, in that order, and form the cacheable prefix.

**What if the embedding model is slow, down, or just changed?**
- **Slow or down:** each search has a time budget (`search_timeout`, default 5 s). On timeout or error, the model is told search is unavailable and continues with the tools it has. A request never fails because of tool search.
- **Just changed:** a new model id changes every cache key, so each node re-embeds an agent's hidden tools in the background when that agent next runs. If the model id stays the same but what's behind it changes (for example, a new connector), entries expire within an hour.

**Why an in-memory cache rather than a system index?**
- **Cheap to recompute:** vectors are cheap to recompute (about 1,000–2,500 tokens of embedding input per agent per node), and pools are small.
- **Less to build:** an index would need `SdkClient` support for multi-tenancy, a mapping, and cleanup of old-model vectors.
- **Tenant isolation:** it comes from the key, which includes the tenant id.
- **Persistence later:** a persistent store can be added later if it's ever needed.

**What happens on the next message in a conversation?**
The run starts again from the pinned tools, plus every configured tool the conversation already called (up to `max_dynamic_tools`). The model can keep using those without searching. The conversation's earlier tool calls always refer to tools in the request.

**Can I change an agent's tool search settings later?**
Yes, with the update agent API. An update changes only the `tool_selection` fields it sets. To turn tool search off, set `enabled` to `false`; null isn't accepted in an update.

**Can repeated searches make the prompt big again?**
No. `max_dynamic_tools` (default 15) caps what a run can append. In round 2, no run added more than 10.

**Which agent types does this cover?**
`conversational_v2` in this RFC. See Scope for the other types and for Agent Skills.

**Can the model call a tool it hasn't been shown?**
Yes, if it names a hidden tool directly (the names are listed in `search_tools`). The call runs, and the tool is appended so its schema is shown from then on. Hiding tools reduces prompt size; it isn't access control.

**Does the result depend on one model?**
Round 2 tested Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Gemini 2.5 Pro.
- **Tokens:** savings were nearly identical (59% and 61% of the all-tools total).
- **Accuracy:** within noise on both.
- **Search path:** stronger on Claude.

items.title: Full product and demo-plan feedback scan (2026-10-24)
items.body:
Tracking issue for a full feedback scan of everything built so far and of the demo plan. It runs ahead of the internal run-through (Sun 2026-11-01) and the external demo (Tue 2026-11-03). The code freeze is 2026-10-29.

A dedicated scan session audits `main` at `c4670a7f` and posts **one** ranked report here. It is read-only: no pushes, PRs or merges. It covers:

1. **The product against its own specs**: the eight P0 pillars (CLAUDE.md, `docs/product/*_SPEC.md`), the ADRs marked Accepted or As built, and STATE.md, against what the code does. That means gaps, half-built features presented as done, and ADR claims the code contradicts.
2. **Security and correctness**: authorization, tenant isolation, secure-by-default settings (ADR-0180), secrets handling, the governance hot path, migrations and data integrity, and supply chain (all lockfiles, including the engine closures).
3. **Reliability and operations**: start-up guards, failure modes, retries and timeouts, observability, backup and restore, the BYOC and air-gapped claims, and CI health and flakiness.
4. **UI/UX and accessibility**: every page in the route census, empty, error and loading states, copy, and the ADR-0196 bars.
5. **The demo plan**: `docs/product/DEMO_SCRIPT_2026-11-01.md`, `DEMO_RUNBOOK.md`, ADR-0197 and ADR-0198. The talk track against the product, the story's strength for the audience, what a sharp evaluator would ask and whether the product answers it, and the fallback and reset paths.
6. **Process**: whether the open-source-first rule (ADR-0176) and the records (STATE, ADR index, mistakes ledger) are being kept.

The report states only what is new or still open. It does not repeat findings from the #522 deep scan that are already fixed. The master session then turns the findings into held fix PRs, each with an independent review. Owner decisions go to #453.

items.body:
## Why
The owner needs Hyperion-96 to be **reconstructible from zero** without remembering historical terminal sessions. Today the configuration is spread across an older local inference repository, a staged-only greenfield repo, machine receipts, private Control Tower execution-source PRs, and cloud/Mac workstation infrastructure. The existence of receipts is **not** a complete rebuild or a clean-restored machine proof.

This is a **Linux host reproducibility and agent documentation acceptance child** of Workstation Bootstrap #18 and Control Tower #349, not a second bootstrap or general-purpose secret exporter.

## Existing evidence and proposed source

- Private, draft Control Tower [PR #1046](https://github.com/pinklon/shareplane-control-tower/pull/1046) is the host-specific reconstruction and recovery baseline, includes a sanitized host metadata collector and a **candidate** cross-agent change receipt contract. It is not yet merged/admitted.
- Existing workstation-manager release/doctor implementation is primarily Mac-oriented. Do not equate Mac conformance with a qualified Hyperion Linux installation.
- Existing Skills owner: `pinklon/skills#323`. Host source and installed profile must reconcile as desired -> selected -> materialized -> invoked -> consumed independently.
- Existing owner compute source: Control Tower #349 and draft PR #1045 (owner-only synthetic job); no external user access admitted.
- Historical local inference state and credentials require separate audited extraction. Never upload raw `~/llmstack` Git history, .env files, credential backups or a raw home-directory archive.

## Acceptance tasks and explicit owners

**Workstation Bootstrap source/maintainer:**
1. Define an owner-approved Linux capability profile for Hyperion under the existing managed Workstation Bootstrap source. Host-specific configurable release inputs, identity, packages, kernels/drivers, distro repos, mounts and runtime versions require exact source identity.
2. Implement dry-run, install, doctor, activation receipt, compatibility and rollback for a **clean Ubuntu host**; preserve current Mac behavior. Do not mutate an active owner machine merely to satisfy CI.
3. Add a host configuration documentation gate: a declared Linux host-affecting change must include an exact signed/owner-admitted change receipt (or explicit disposition), source+actual version+verification, secret-handling classification, rollback and updated rebuild guide. Reuse existing receipt contracts, don't invent another authority.
4. Test a clean VM installation twice and ensure results are deterministic or differences explicitly documented.

**Hyperion host administrator (privilege/maintenance approval required):**
5. Inventory disk UUID and firmware/boot dependencies privately, verify and **restore from an independently off-host encrypted backup**, including WebUI assets, model weights, historical artifacts, and key re-enrollment path. Store no keys in public source.
6. Qualify remote-access reconnect from at least two independent Macs, NoMachine or VNC current surface, clipboard, audio and file transfer, and reboot persistence with out-of-band recovery.
7. Reconcile GPU driver 595 to separately planned qualified Blackwell stack, host firewall/SSH/Tailscale/desktop ingress and safe rollback without exposing tenant access.

**Skills/Control Tower conformance owners:**
8. Compare canonical Skills exact SHA/digest to scoped installed and actual runtime consumption; keep Production and external compute gates separate.
9. Enforce or check sanitized documentation receipts across active Hyperion writer lanes and issue claim closeout. Merely documenting policy does not establish agent-wide compliance.
10. Have an independent witness perform cold restore into a clean host/VM and score every service outcome PASS/FAIL/UNOBSERVED.

## Terminal criteria

Only close when a third party can rebuild without chat archaeology using:
- versioned source + immutable artifact lock manifest,
- explicit non-secret dependency/credential enrollment instructions,
- retained off-host backup and verified restore,
- transactional installer plus rollback,
- exact acceptance tests and reboot-persistence results,
- desired-versus-actual-versus-consumed capability proof,
- source/host/agent receipt reconciliation,
- no private value leaked to the repository or logs.

**Current disposition: OPEN. No claim of reproducible rebuild, global agent compliance, or tenant-ready compute.**

items.title: [RFC] OpenSearch Memory API: events and memories for AI agents
items.body:
## What are you proposing?

Agent memory has evolved rapidly across the industry. Agents used to keep a chat history. More and more, they keep facts, summaries, and preferences that a large language model (LLM) extracts from conversations, carry them across sessions and agents, and act on them. As memory moves from a log of messages to knowledge an agent relies on, applications need three things that today's memory APIs do not give together:

- **Lineage.** Knowing which conversation each memory came from, so it can be checked, corrected, or deleted with its source.
- **Configurability.** Choosing, for each application, what gets extracted, with which prompt and model, how long raw records and memories are kept, and who can read and change them.
- **The raw record.** Keeping the original conversation searchable, because extraction leaves details out.

This RFC proposes a new memory API for OpenSearch, under `/_plugins/_memory`, built around those needs. It stores two kinds of records in a **Space**, which holds an application's extraction strategies, models, expiry settings, and access:

- **Events.** What an agent or application writes: conversation turns, agent state, tool results, or any JSON document. Events are kept as written and never change.
- **Memories.** What an LLM extracts from events in the background: facts, session summaries, user preferences, or whatever a custom prompt asks for. Each memory records the events it came from. An application can also write memories it extracts itself.

The API is **experimental**: it is off unless a cluster turns it on with a static setting, and it can change between releases until the community agrees it is stable. This RFC does not decide where the code lives. It could be part of the ML Commons plugin, or a dedicated plugin that calls ML Commons for models, as the Neural Search plugin does; the API design does not depend on the answer.

## What problems are you trying to solve?

An agent's memory holds two kinds of records: what happened, such as conversation turns, tool results, and agent state, and what an LLM inferred from it, such as facts, summaries, and preferences. The two need different rules. Raw records should never change, while inferred ones are updated as new turns refine them. They need their own lifetimes and their own permissions. Each inference also needs a link back to the records it came from, so a detail it left out can still be found, and so it can be deleted with its conversation. Agentic memory does not keep the two apart, as the next section shows. This RFC makes them two resources, events and memories, linked by lineage.

## Why events and memories are separate resources

An event is something that happened. A memory is something an LLM inferred from what happened. The two differ in who writes them, whether they can change, how long they are kept, and how they are found:

|  | Event | Memory |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | A raw record: a conversation turn, agent state, a tool result, or a JSON document | An inference: a fact, a summary, a preference, or the output of a custom prompt |
| Who writes it | The agent or application | The extraction pipeline, or the application with CreateMemory |
| How it is made | Stored exactly as sent | An LLM call, which is not deterministic |
| Can it change? | No | Yes. Consolidation updates it when new events refine it, and the application can update or delete it |
| How long it is kept | Usually short: days to months (`event_expiry_days`) | Usually long: months to years, or forever (`memory_expiry_days`) |
| Typical size | A whole turn or document | A sentence or a paragraph |
| How it is found | By session and time, by ID, or by keyword and vector search over its chunks | By keyword and vector search, filtered by actor and strategy |

The relationship between them is many to many:

- One event can produce several memories of different types, for example a fact, an updated session summary, and a user preference.
- One event can produce no new memory, when consolidation finds that existing memories already cover it.
- One memory can come from several events, when consolidation merges what they said.

**Lineage.** Every memory records the events it came from in `source_event_ids`. That link supports a two-step retrieval pattern. An agent searches memories first, which returns a few short records instead of whole conversations. If a memory lacks the detail the agent needs, such as the exact error message or the full list a user gave, the agent follows `source_event_ids` to the original events. The link also works the other way: a memory search can filter by `source_event_ids`, so an application can find every memory that came from given events and delete them. Events are usually kept for less time than the memories made from them; once an event is deleted, BatchGetEvent reports its ID as not found.

**How agentic memory models this.** Agentic memory in ML Commons keeps both under one memory container API, with the raw records as one memory type (working memory) and the extracted records as another (long-term memory), next to sessions and history. The same paths and fields then serve records with different lifetimes and rules: working memory can be edited after it is written, and a long-term memory does not reference the messages it came from.

Agent memory systems commonly call these two kinds of records short-term memory and long-term memory. In this API, short-term memory is events, and long-term memory is memories.

## Why a new API, and how it relates to agentic memory

The ML Commons plugin has two memory APIs today: conversation memory and agentic memory. Given that conversation memory is on the deprecation path ([maintainer comment on ml-commons#4552](https://github.com/opensearch-project/ml-commons/issues/4552#issuecomment-3844465824)), this RFC mainly compares the new memory API with agentic memory. The section "Long-term direction: one memory API" describes the proposal to converge on one.

Agentic memory (experimental in 3.2, generally available in 3.3, `/_plugins/_ml/memory_containers`) stores messages in memory containers and extracts long-term memories from them. ML Commons agents use it, and other applications can call it directly.

Another API has a real cost: more code to maintain, and more for users to choose between. We propose it because the event and memory model changes the data model of agentic memory, not just its features:

- **Two record types instead of four.** Agentic memory has sessions, working memory, long-term memory, and history, each under the same generic paths. Splitting them into events and memories changes its paths.
- **Raw records that never change.** Agentic memory's working memory can be updated. Making it immutable breaks callers that update it.
- **Fixed actor and session fields on every record.** Agentic memory scopes records with namespace keys that each strategy chooses, such as `user_id`. A strategy whose key is missing from a write is skipped. Replacing namespaces with two fixed fields changes every request and response.
- **A link from every memory to its events.** This part is additive, and agentic memory could add it on its own.

Changing agentic memory this way would break its current users, including ML Commons agents. A new, experimental API leaves both existing APIs as they are, and lets the new model prove itself before anything is deprecated.

The table compares the three:

| Area | Memory API (proposed) | Agentic memory | Conversation memory |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Containers and records | A Space holds events and memories | A memory container holds four memory types: sessions, working, long-term, and history | A memory holds one conversation's messages, each an input and a response, with optional traces |
| User and session | Every event and memory has an `actor_id` and an optional `session_id` | Each strategy names the namespace keys it needs, for example `user_id`, or `agent_id` and `session_id` | One memory per conversation, owned by the OpenSearch user who created it |
| Long-term memories | Extracted by an LLM, or written by the client | Extracted by an LLM | None |
| Source of a memory | Each memory records `source_event_ids`, and memory search can filter by them | Not recorded | Not applicable |
| Updating a raw record | No. Events cannot be changed | Yes, working memory can be updated | Yes, messages can be updated |
| Consolidation | Yes | Yes. For each new fact, the LLM decides to add, update, or delete against similar stored memories (`max_infer_size`, 5 by default, at most 10), and a history index records each change | Not applicable |
| Search over raw records | Keyword, semantic, and hybrid | Keyword only. Working memory is not embedded | Keyword only |
| Search over memories | Keyword, semantic, and hybrid | Keyword, semantic, and hybrid. Semantic queries since 3.3; dedicated semantic and hybrid APIs since 3.6 | Not applicable |
| Expiry | Per Space, for events and for memories. An expired memory is left out of reads before it is deleted | Since 3.8, with age and count limits and pinning. On-demand runs and a dry run since 3.9. An expired record is returned until the retention job deletes it | None |
| Strategies | SEMANTIC, SUMMARY, and CUSTOM | SEMANTIC, USER_PREFERENCE, and SUMMARY, each with an optional custom prompt | None |

The new API starts with a focused feature set. Features that agentic memory has, such as a change history, delete by query, per-request hybrid weights, count limits and pinning in retention, a built-in user-preference strategy, and checkpoint fields, can be added based on community interest.

**What changes in existing components:**

| Component | Change |
| --- | --- |
| ML Commons plugin | Either it hosts the new API, or it is called through its client for model predictions, as the Neural Search and Flow Framework plugins call it. Its two memory APIs do not change. With a dedicated plugin, it adds a memory type extension point for agents (see "Long-term direction") |
| Security plugin | None required. When it is installed, Spaces can be registered with its resource sharing framework |
| k-NN and Neural Search plugins | None. The k-NN plugin provides vector fields, and the Neural Search plugin provides the `text_chunking` processor and `neural` and `hybrid` queries |
| Job Scheduler plugin | None. The implementation registers its own jobs for the extraction backlog and for expiry |
| OpenSearch core | None |

## What is the developer experience going to be?

### Use cases

Some common use cases for the API:

- When an agent needs a detail from earlier turns, such as an error code, a file name, or a value a user gave, the agent developer wants to search the raw turns by keyword and by meaning, so the agent finds the exact detail even when no extracted memory kept it.
- When memories go stale or a retention rule applies, the developer wants events and memories to expire after a set time, so old memories stop shaping answers and data is not kept longer than allowed.
- When an agent resumes a session or restarts, the agent developer wants to reload the session's recent turns, so the conversation continues where it left off.
- When a user returns to an agent in a new session, the agent developer wants the agent to recall facts and preferences from earlier sessions, so the user does not repeat them.
- When a conversation runs long, the developer wants a running summary of the whole session, so the agent can keep context without sending every turn to the model.
- When an application serves more than one end user, the developer wants each end user's memories stored under that user's ID and searchable by user and session, so the application shows each user only their own memories.
- When an agent needs a detail a memory left out, or an application must show where a memory came from or delete what a conversation produced, the developer wants each memory linked to the events it came from, so the agent can read the original turns and the application can check or delete memories by their source.

### Experimental status

The API is off by default. A cluster turns it on with a static setting in `opensearch.yml`, for example `plugins.memory.experimental.enabled: true`. The final name follows from where the code lives. With the setting off, the memory paths do not exist.

While the API is experimental:

- It can change in breaking ways between releases. The release notes list every change, and any step needed for data written by an earlier release.
- The documentation marks it with one notice: "Experimental: this API can change between releases until it is marked stable."
- It does not replace or change the ML Commons memory APIs.

### Resources

- **Space.** A container for one application's memory. It holds the memory strategies, the ML Commons model used for extraction (`extraction_model_id`), the ML Commons model used for vectors (`embedding_model_id`), and how long to keep events (`event_expiry_days`, default 90) and memories (`memory_expiry_days`, default 365, where 0 means never). Without an extraction model, a Space stores events and extracts nothing. Without an embedding model, search is by keyword only. The embedding model cannot be changed after the Space is created, because stored vectors would no longer match. A Space with an embedding model also gives `embedding_dimension`, the size of the model's vectors.
- **Event.** One conversation turn, a group of turns, or a JSON document. An event has an actor ID (for example, the end user), an optional session ID, a timestamp, the payload, and string key-value pairs of metadata.
- **Memory.** A record extracted from events by a strategy, or written directly with CreateMemory. Each memory belongs to one strategy, one actor, and optionally one session, and records the events it came from in `source_event_ids`.

### Strategies

A strategy tells the extraction pipeline what to extract. Two types ship with built-in prompts, and `CUSTOM` brings its own:

| Type | What it extracts |
| --- | --- |
| `SEMANTIC` | Facts stated in the conversation, as short standalone statements |
| `SUMMARY` | One running summary per session, updated with each event |
| `CUSTOM` | Whatever the strategy's `extraction_prompt` asks for, for example user preferences |

On any strategy, `configuration.consolidation_enabled` turns consolidation with stored memories on or off. Strategies read a JSON event as JSON text.

### Operations

All paths are under `/_plugins/_memory`, whichever plugin serves them.

| Operation | Method and path |
| --- | --- |
| CreateSpace | `POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces` |
| GetSpace | `GET /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}` |
| UpdateSpace | `PUT /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}` |
| DeleteSpace | `DELETE /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}` |
| ListSpaces | `GET /_plugins/_memory/spaces` |
| CreateEvent | `POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/events` |
| GetEvent | `GET /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/events/{event_id}` |
| BatchGetEvent | `POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/events/_mget` |
| ListEvents | `POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/events/_list` |
| SearchEvents | `POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/events/_search` |
| DeleteEvent | `DELETE /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/events/{event_id}` |
| CreateMemory | `POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/memories` |
| GetMemory | `GET /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/memories/{memory_id}` |
| UpdateMemory | `PUT /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/memories/{memory_id}` |
| DeleteMemory | `DELETE /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/memories/{memory_id}` |
| ListMemories | `POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/memories/_list` |
| SearchMemories | `POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/memories/_search` |
| Node statistics | `GET /_plugins/_memory/stats` |

Reads are scoped by actor and session:

- ListEvents requires one `actor_id` and one `session_id`.
- SearchEvents and SearchMemories require one `actor_id`, and accept an optional list of `session_ids`.
- ListMemories accepts optional lists of `actor_ids` and `session_ids`.
- GetEvent, BatchGetEvent, and the memory get, update, and delete operations accept the actor, and the session for events, as optional scope checks. A record outside the scope answers as not found.

Request options:

- CreateSpace, CreateEvent, and CreateMemory accept a `client_token`, so a retried write is stored once and the retry returns the stored record.
- CreateEvent accepts `infer: false` to store an event without extracting memories from it.
- List and search operations take `max_results` for the page size, and return a `next_token` for the next page.
- ListEvents and ListMemories take their filters in a request body, sent with `POST` to `_list`.
- CreateEvent and UpdateMemory accept `refresh` (`wait_for` by default, `true`, or `false`). Other writes, except CreateMemory, always wait for the refresh.

### Example

Create a Space with three strategies:

```json
POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces
{
  "name": "support-assistant",
  "memory_strategies": [
    { "type": "SEMANTIC", "name": "facts" },
    { "type": "SUMMARY", "name": "session_summary" },
    {
      "type": "CUSTOM",
      "name": "preferences",
      "configuration": {
        "extraction_prompt": "List the user's stated preferences, one per line.",
        "consolidation_enabled": true
      }
    }
  ],
  "extraction_model_id": "<ML Commons model ID>",
  "embedding_model_id": "<ML Commons model ID>",
  "embedding_dimension": 1024,
  "event_expiry_days": 90,
  "memory_expiry_days": 365
}
```

Write a conversation turn:

```json
POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/events
{
  "actor_id": "user-123",
  "session_id": "session-1",
  "payload": {
    "conversational": {
      "unified": {
        "source": {
          "object": {
            "messages": [
              { "role": "USER", "content": { "text": "I always want a window seat." } },
              { "role": "ASSISTANT", "content": { "text": "Got it. I'll book window seats from now on." } }
            ]
          }
        }
      }
    }
  },
  "metadata": { "channel": "web" }
}
```

The event is stored, the call answers `201 Created`, and memories are extracted in the background. Later, in a new session:

```json
POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/memories/_search
{
  "actor_id": "user-123",
  "query": { "match": { "memory_text": "seat" } },
  "max_results": 5
}
```

Each result carries `source_event_ids`, so the agent can read the original turns with BatchGetEvent when it needs more detail.

The `conversational.unified.source.object` levels leave room for other payload kinds and sources. Search takes `query` at the top level of the body, as `_search` does. The Space, actor, and session filters are separate fields, so a query cannot widen them.

## Long-term direction: one memory API

We propose that OpenSearch converge on one memory API. This RFC asks only for agreement on the event and memory model as an experimental API. How and when the two APIs converge is decided with the ML Commons maintainers once the new API is stable. Before agentic memory is deprecated, the new API needs to support existing memory workloads, with a compatibility bridge that keeps existing data usable through the new API or a way to move that data into Spaces.

ML Commons agents can use a Space through a memory type. In ML Commons, this is a new memory type next to `AGENTIC_MEMORY`. In a dedicated plugin, ML Commons will add a memory type extension point, which we would contribute; ML Commons still runs without the plugin. Saving to a Space calls no model in the agent's request; extraction runs later in the memory API's own thread pool.

Agent runtimes outside ML Commons can use the new API from the experimental release:

- The [OpenSearch Agent Server](https://github.com/opensearch-project/opensearch-agent-server), for its threads, runs, messages, and events.
- Framework integrations, such as the Strands session manager requested in [.github#443](https://github.com/opensearch-project/.github/issues/443) and the Strands store in [ml-commons#4919](https://github.com/opensearch-project/ml-commons/issues/4919).
- The memory tools in [opensearch-mcp-server-py](https://github.com/opensearch-project/opensearch-mcp-server-py).
- Checkpoint stores for agent frameworks, such as [LangGraph checkpointers](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/concepts/persistence/).

## How it works

This section outlines one implementation. It holds whether the code lives in the ML Commons plugin or in a dedicated plugin.

Diagram 1 shows how an event is stored, how its text is chunked and embedded, how memories are extracted and consolidated, how searches are served, and how records expire. Numbered arrows are the write path, blue arrows are searches, and dashed boxes and arrows run in the background.

<img width="3820" height="2200" alt="Image" src="https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/254636cf-59ec-4b8f-a0e0-3da958810e35" />

*Diagram 1. How the Memory API works on a cluster.*

- **Storage.** Spaces, events, event chunks, and memories live in four system indexes: `.plugins-memory-spaces`, `.plugins-memory-events`, `.plugins-memory-event-chunks`, and `.plugins-memory-memories`. The Job Scheduler jobs live in `.plugins-memory-jobs`. Each event is one document: the full payload, kept as written but not indexed, and a text field with its messages. Each chunk of an event's text is its own document in the chunks index, with the event's ID, Space, actor, session, timestamp, and metadata. Deleting or expiring an event deletes its chunks. Every document stores its Space ID, and its tenant ID when multi-tenancy is on. A get, update, or delete by ID compares the document's Space with the Space in the request and answers 404 on a mismatch, and every search and list filters on the Space. IDs that come from a caller or a model, such as `source_event_ids` or the memories consolidation changes, are checked the same way. Spaces whose embedding models need different vector settings, such as the vector size, use separate chunk and memory indexes. Each index mapping carries a schema version, and older indexes are upgraded in place when a new release adds fields. Application metadata is stored in a `flat_object` field, so the keys an application chooses do not add fields to the shared index mappings.
- **Chunking and embedding.** CreateEvent splits the event's text into chunks by running the Neural Search plugin's `text_chunking` processor through the ingest simulate API, which needs no code dependency on Neural Search, then writes the event and one document per chunk in a single bulk request, so keyword search finds the event at once. Chunk IDs are derived from the event ID, so a retry with the same `client_token` rewrites the same chunks. When a Space names an embedding model, the background work calls it through ML Commons predict and adds a vector to each chunk, so a slow or unavailable model never delays or fails the write. If embedding fails, the Space's backlog job retries it. Event search runs on the chunks index, so each result is one matching chunk with the ID of its event. Extraction embeds each memory before storing it, so consolidation can compare it with stored memories at once. Memories written with CreateMemory get their vector in the background, like chunks. UpdateMemory re-embeds changed content before it returns.
- **Extraction.** Extraction runs on the cluster, in its own bounded thread pool, so there is no second process to deploy. Models are called through ML Commons predict as the implementation's own identity, and only with the model IDs stored on the Space. Whoever sets a Space's models must be allowed to use them. SUMMARY updates one summary per session from the stored summary and the new event, so the summary covers the whole session. Each memory records every event it came from in `source_event_ids`. Consolidation compares a new memory only with memories of the same Space, actor, and strategy, and the model can update or delete only those memories.
- **Extraction under load.** The node that receives an event runs its extraction in the bounded thread pool. Every event stays marked pending until its extraction finishes, so the backlog job retries work lost when a node stops, up to a set number of tries. Each Space has a Job Scheduler job that picks up the Space's pending events on a configurable interval, one minute by default. Job Scheduler runs each job on one of the data nodes that hold a copy of the job's shard, under a lock, so only one node works on a Space's backlog at a time, and the cluster manager node does no extraction. Index State Management, Anomaly Detection, Alerting, and agentic memory's retention job use the same pattern.
- **Search.** Event search and memory search accept only query types whose cost is bounded and that never read other documents: `match`, `match_phrase`, `match_all`, `term`, `terms` (values only), `ids`, `exists`, `bool`, `constant_score`, `boosting`, `range` and `function_score` decay on the time fields, and, when the Space has an embedding model, `neural` and `hybrid`. The implementation checks every clause against that list before the query runs, and rejects anything else with 400. It adds the Space, actor, and session filters itself, inside each `neural` and `hybrid` clause as well as around the query, so a query cannot widen its scope, and a semantic search still finds the closest matches within it. `neural` always uses the Space's embedding model, and `hybrid` scores are combined by a normalization search pipeline that the implementation creates. Both searches can filter by the application's metadata under `metadata.<key>`, and memory search can also filter by `source_event_ids`.
- **Read-after-write.** By default, CreateEvent and UpdateMemory return after the next refresh (`refresh=wait_for`), so a get, list, or keyword search that follows sees the write. CreateMemory answers 202 with the new memory's ID and stores the memory in the background; GetMemory finds it once it is indexed. Semantic search sees a new event once its vectors are added.
- **Expiry.** A Job Scheduler job deletes events older than `event_expiry_days`, with their chunks, and memories older than `memory_expiry_days`. A memory's age counts from when the implementation last wrote it; UpdateMemory does not reset it. An expired memory reads as not found, even before the job deletes it.
- **Running next to the ML Commons memory APIs.** The new API shares no path, index, setting, or permission with the ML Commons memory APIs, so they can run on the same cluster at the same time, and an application can move from one to another at its own pace.

## What is the user experience going to be?

- A cluster administrator turns on the experimental setting, and connects a model through ML Commons.
- A developer creates a Space and starts writing events. Memories are extracted and appear without further calls.
- Optionally, the application writes memories it extracts itself with CreateMemory, using any model or framework it already has, and a single event can skip extraction with `infer: false`.

## Are there any security considerations?

The API relies on the Security plugin for access control. Cluster admins, and the front end that sets the tenant ID, are trusted. OpenSearch users, usually applications, are kept apart per Space. End users do not call the API; their text is untrusted input to the models, and it leaves the cluster for the configured model providers.

- **Permissions.** Each operation is its own transport action, so Security plugin roles can grant operations one by one. Changing a Space's models or prompts, and searching SUMMARY or CUSTOM memories, can reveal event text, so those permissions count as read access to events.
- **Space access.** A Space is private to its owner and to admins (`all_access`) by default. The owner shares it through a `backend_roles` field: a user who holds one of those backend roles can use the Space. Only the owner or an admin can change `backend_roles`, the models, the strategies and prompts, and the expiry settings, and a user who is not an admin can add only backend roles they hold.
- **Records inside a Space.** Access is checked per Space, not per record. A user who can use a Space can read all of its events and memories. Agentic memory, by contrast, limits users who are not admins to the records they wrote. The `actor_id` and `session_id` on a request narrow what it returns, but the application supplies them, so they are not an access check.
- **Tenant isolation.** With multi-tenancy on, the REST layer reads the tenant ID from the `x-tenant-id` header, as ML Commons does, and every Space lookup checks it. The header is trusted as sent, so a deployment must set it from the caller's authenticated identity in a front end, and drop any value the client sends.
- **System indexes.** The memory indexes are system indexes. With the Security plugin, they are closed to users only when `plugins.security.system_indices.enabled` is true, which is off by default, so the implementation warns at startup when it is off. Even then, the super-admin certificate, roles granted `system:admin/system_index`, and snapshot restores can read every Space. Without the Security plugin, there is no access control.
- **Models.** ML Commons connectors hold the model credentials; the memory indexes store none. Event text goes to whatever endpoint a Space's models call, which is why only the owner or an admin can change the models, and the ML Commons setting `plugins.ml_commons.trusted_connector_endpoints_regex` limits where connectors can send it.
- **Model input.** Event text goes into the extraction prompt, and memories are later returned to agents, so text in an event can steer what is stored. Applications need to treat memories as user input. Each event write causes model calls, so a busy writer raises model cost for the whole cluster. ML Commons model rate limits, when set, cap it.

We also propose registering Spaces with the Security plugin's [resource sharing framework](https://docs.opensearch.org/latest/security/access-control/resources/), so an owner can share one Space with specific users, roles, or backend roles. When the framework is on for Spaces, it alone decides who can use a Space; otherwise the backend-role rule above does. The two are never combined.

## Are there any breaking changes to the API and User Experience?

No. The API adds new paths under `/_plugins/_memory`, which exist only when the experimental setting is on. The ML Commons memory APIs, `/_plugins/_ml/memory` and `/_plugins/_ml/memory_containers`, do not change.

## Why should it be built? Any reason not to?

**Why build it:**

- **One memory API for every agent runtime.** Agent state is kept in several places today: agentic memory, the OpenSearch Agent Server's own SQLite store of threads, runs, messages, and events, and each framework adapter. One API lets a memory written by one runtime be read by another.
- **Search over the raw conversation.** Events are indexed for keyword search, and for semantic and hybrid search when a Space names an embedding model, so an agent can find a detail that extraction did not keep.
- **Memories that trace back to their source.** Every memory records the events it came from, whether it was extracted or written with CreateMemory. The link is used to fetch a memory's source events, audit where it came from, and delete what a conversation produced.
- **Safe retries.** A retried write with the same `client_token` is stored once.

**Alternatives we considered:**

- **Change agentic memory to the event and memory model.** Rejected because it breaks agentic memory users, as the section "Why a new API" describes.
- **A client library on top of agentic memory**, as [ml-commons#4919](https://github.com/opensearch-project/ml-commons/issues/4919) and [.github#443](https://github.com/opensearch-project/.github/issues/443) propose for Strands. Rejected because the differences are on the server: the source links, the immutable events, and the actor and session fields. A client library cannot add them.

**Reasons not to:**

- **"I don't think we want to implement memory management twice"** ([ml-commons#1150](https://github.com/opensearch-project/ml-commons/issues/1150)). This is the main cost. OpenSearch would have two memory APIs that extract long-term memories until they converge. The long-term direction proposes converging them on one API, with a compatibility bridge that keeps existing data usable or a way to move it into Spaces.
- **More memory APIs confuse users.** The experimental setting means nobody adopts the new API by accident, and the documentation will say which API fits which need until agentic memory is deprecated.
- **Agentic memory has more features today.** The new API starts with a focused set, and features can be added based on community interest.

## What will it take to execute?

- **Dependencies.** The ML Commons plugin for model calls, the Job Scheduler plugin for the extraction backlog and expiry, the Neural Search plugin for chunking and for `neural` and `hybrid` queries, the k-NN plugin for vector fields, and optionally the Security plugin.
- **Versions.** The API runs its background work under its own plugin identity, which needs the Security plugin fix that lets a plugin identity use its own system indexes ([security#5858](https://github.com/opensearch-project/security/pull/5858), in 3.5). If the code lives in ML Commons, ML Commons first adopts plugin identity.
- **Clients.** The API is added to opensearch-api-specification after it is implemented, so clients can be generated from it.
- **Cost.** Each event leads to model calls for each strategy: one to extract, one to consolidate when consolidation is on, and embedding calls when the Space has an embedding model. The implementation can batch these calls, such as several turns of a session in one extraction call, without changing the API.
- **Process.** This RFC, open for community review. If the community chooses a dedicated plugin, a repository request and the project's security review for a new repository follow.

## Any remaining open questions?

We would like the community's view on these questions:

1. **Where should the code live?** The API design is the same either way.

   - *In the ML Commons plugin*, next to the existing memory APIs. No new repository, release pipeline, or set of maintainers. Changes are reviewed in the existing ML Commons community and its weekly meeting, where backward compatibility is already checked. Other plugins already call ML Commons through a small client layer.
   - *In a dedicated plugin* that calls ML Commons for models, as the Neural Search and Flow Framework plugins do. Memory gets its own owners and an optional install, and ML Commons stays focused on models and inference, a split proposed for memory in 2023 ([ml-commons#1150](https://github.com/opensearch-project/ml-commons/issues/1150#issuecomment-1666021113)) and for agents in [.github#398](https://github.com/opensearch-project/.github/issues/398). The cost is another repository to build, release, and secure.
   - *Paths.* We propose `/_plugins/_memory` in both cases, so the answer does not change the API. If the community prefers ML Commons' own prefix when the code lives there, the same operations would sit under it, for example `/_plugins/_ml/spaces/{space_id}/events`. `/_plugins/_ml/memory` is taken by conversation memory.
2. **Agentic memory.** What should the path to one API look like, and would ML Commons add the memory type extension point described in "Long-term direction"? The existing `REMOTE_AGENTIC_MEMORY` memory type calls fixed agentic memory paths ([ml-commons#4572](https://github.com/opensearch-project/ml-commons/issues/4572)), so it cannot reach a Space as it stands.
3. **Leaving experimental status.** What should the API show before it becomes stable: a number of releases without breaking changes, use by ML Commons agents, or a benchmark of extraction quality?

Out of scope for this RFC: OpenSearch Dashboards support and framework adapters (LangChain, LlamaIndex, and Strands). With a dedicated plugin, the memory type extension point would be its own ML Commons change.
