# 13. Separate problem: global lifecycle of `dialer`

`EnableCounting` is process-global and one-shot.

The first production bootstrap studied is correctly ordered:

```text
state.New
    -> EnableCounting
    -> datastore/connections/warehouse
```

Lambda is constructed earlier but creates its client lazily.

So the current first bootstrap is not merely a fragile convention: the composition root studied orders it correctly.

## 13.1 Problem with subsequent lifecycles

There remain, however, cases incompatible with the global state:

### Core #1 counting ON -> Close -> Core #2 counting ON

The second `EnableCounting` may panic.

### Core #1 counting ON -> Close -> Core #2 counting OFF

The global flag may remain active, and the second lifecycle may see registries belonging to the first.

### `core.New` fails after `EnableCounting`

A retry in the same process may find `dialer` already initialized.

This problem must be solved separately from HTTP pooling.

---

# 14. Caution: making `dialer` instance-scoped is not just "putting the maps in a struct"

The future redesign must account for two details that the first API draft risked hiding.

## 14.1 State listeners

`state.AddListener` does not currently expose a regular API for removing listeners.

If a future instance-scoped `Dialer` registers listeners:

- its owner must live at least as long as the state; or
- a consistent lifecycle/unsubscribe must be introduced.

A plain `Dialer.Close()` is not enough if the listeners keep calling the instance after it is closed.

## 14.2 Prometheus collector

The metric family/counter vector is by nature registered at the process level.

Even when moving:

```text
organization -> counter
```

into an instance, the following must be defined carefully:

- who registers/unregisters the labels;
- what happens between two sequential `Core`s;
- what happens on init failure;
- how to avoid stale counters;
- how to handle the recreation of an organization;
- how to keep the same metric family without double registrations.

So the direction:

```text
state-scoped Dialer
```

remains recommended, but it requires a real design of the State + listener + Prometheus lifecycle.

---

# 15. Current temporal semantics not to lose sight of

The fixed dialers and `DialWithContext` currently do not have the same temporal semantics.

## Fixed organization

`Dial`/`DialWith` resolve the counter when the dialer/decorator is built.

Consequences:

- a dialer built with counting disabled stays plain;
- a dialer built for a nonexistent organization stays plain even if that ID is created later;
- after delete, an existing dialer may retain the pointer to the old counter; the counter is unregistered and subsequent writes are no longer collected.

## Context dialer

`DialWithContext` resolves membership/counter on every new dial.

After the future redesign, it must be decided deliberately which of these semantics to keep.

For fixed-org consumers, the owner's affinity/lifetime makes a fixed scope natural.

For the dynamic HTTP router, it is instead preferable to re-evaluate membership on every request, not just on every dial.

---

# 16. Organization identity, unknown, deleted, and plain

This distinction is critical.

The current `WithOrganization` only validates that the ID is not empty.

A future HTTP router must not use the context as the authority for creating resources.

## 16.1 Valid organization

A regular organization-required path must create/use a pool only if the ID is recognized by a trusted source, normally the state.

```text
known organization
    -> counted pool when counting ON
```

## 16.2 Counting disabled

The regular path can keep validating the organization but share a plain pool:

```text
known A
known B
    -> shared uncounted pool
```

provided there are no other isolation requirements.

The optimization must not change the caller's contract.

## 16.3 Missing context

In an organization-required client:

```text
missing organization
    -> immediate error
```

It must not silently become plain.

## 16.4 Arbitrary unknown ID

An arbitrary ID in the context:

```text
"some-random-id"
```

must not:

- allocate an entry in the cache;
- create a transport;
- automatically become an accounting bypass.

It must fail or be handled by an explicitly uncounted mode defined by the caller.

## 16.5 Deleted organization / cleanup

Post-delete cleanup is a real case for Lambda.

The PoC demonstrated that it is technically valid:

```text
request already in-flight
    -> completes on the old transport

new cleanup operation
    -> plain/uncounted transport
```

But the future design must not confuse:

```text
trusted deleted organization cleanup
```

with:

```text
arbitrary unknown ID
```

The uncounted mode must be **explicit** or based on a trusted lifecycle/tombstone.

## 16.6 System/plain traffic

System/control-plane traffic must use an explicit plain API/mode, separate from the regular organization-required path.

---

# 17. HTTP pool lifecycle: points to define

The PoC demonstrated that the lifecycle is technically manageable, but the production API must specify its ownership.

## 17.1 Creation

Lazy is preferable:

```text
first request A
    -> create Transport A
```

Creation must happen only once under concurrency.

## 17.2 Delete

Remove the cache entry and call:

```go
CloseIdleConnections()
```

without interrupting requests already in flight.

## 17.3 Fixed facade and stale reference

This is a decision to make explicit in the design.

If an API directly returns:

```text
RoundTripper bound to A
```

the caller can keep it even after the entry is removed from the cache.

So it must be established whether:

- the fixed-org consumer's lifecycle guarantees that the facade is closed/discarded on delete;
- the facade rechecks membership on every request;
- or the current semantics of already-created clients is accepted, where they may finish/continue with an unregistered counter.

Do not assume that `RemoveOrganization` automatically makes every already handed-out reference unusable.

## 17.4 Recreation of the same ID

After delete + create of the same ID, the new owner must use:

- a new transport;
- a new scope/counter;

and must not reactivate stale references.

## 17.5 Shutdown

The future HTTP owner must close all idle pools on `Core.Close`.

The current generic HTTP manager has no explicit `Close`; Lambda does not need one today because keep-alive is disabled.

This changes when Lambda gets persistent pools.

## 17.6 Failed initialization

Constructors should preferably be side-effect-light and caches lazy.

If the new owner registers listeners, the rollback must be defined and idempotent.

---

# 18. Limits of the `http.Transport.Clone` model

For the consumers studied as candidates for the new layer, `*http.Transport.Clone()` is sufficient.

In the domains to be migrated, the study found no production use of:

- `DialTLSContext`;
- `DialTLS`;
- `RegisterProtocol`;
- custom alternate protocols;
- custom non-`*http.Transport` as the router's base.

This must not, however, become an invisible assumption.

The future HTTP layer must:

1. clearly document the supported transport shape;
2. validate or reject configurations that can bypass `DialContext`;
3. have contract tests if the following are added in the future:
   - `DialTLSContext`;
   - HTTP/3/QUIC;
   - special connection upgrades;
   - non-clonable custom RoundTrippers.

`Clone` must be performed on a fully configured base and before applying the fixed-organization wrapper.

A transport already wrapped for an organization must not be cloned as a template.

---

# 19. Retry, redirect, and context propagation

For dynamic HTTP routing, the organization must reach every `RoundTrip`.

The studies verified that:

- the current generic HTTP client preserves the request context during retry/OAuth;
- application connectors use requests built with the caller's context;
- Lambda propagates the same context through the SDK/Smithy;
- the PoC goes through the real AWS client.

The future layer must keep this property as a contract test.

For fixed-org consumers, a bound facade is preferable when possible, because it reduces the dependency on the context and therefore the risk of omission.

---

# 20. Relaxation opportunities

Per-organization pooling is not a dogma.

It is required for correctness when:

```text
connection
    -> holds a counter of an organization
```

and the same infrastructure could serve different organizations.

It can be relaxed when:

## Counting OFF

Multiple organizations can share a plain pool within the same configuration domain, if there are no other isolation requirements.

## Explicit uncounted/system

It can use shared pools according to the configuration domain.

## Deleted cleanup

It can use a plain shared pool if the isolation policy allows it.

## Rare/ephemeral traffic

No-keepalive remains a perfectly valid policy when reuse does not offer enough value.

`DisableKeepAlives` is therefore not "wrong": it must not, however, be required as an implicit workaround for the correctness of a shared counted client.

---

# 21. Resource bounds to decide before the rollout

A pool per organization introduces state proportional to:

```text
active organizations using a configuration domain
×
endpoints/hosts
×
allowed idle connections
```

The current defaults are not necessarily suitable when multiplied by many tenants.

Data to collect before sizing:

- simultaneously active organizations;
- Lambda/application/S3 concurrency;
- distinct hosts;
- idle lifetime;
- file descriptor limit;
- distribution of requests over time.

Do not freeze a universal cap in the common package.

The limits must be able to belong to the base transport/configuration domain.

---

# 22. Proposed direction: new `dialer`

The future API **is not yet frozen**.

The desired responsibility is:

> **connection accounting for an already determined organization.**

The package should progressively:

- remove the process-global lifecycle;
- explicitly represent a fixed-organization scope;
- offer:
  - direct dial;
  - a decorator for the base dialer;
- preserve the base's timeout/resolver/local address/tracing;
- know nothing about HTTP requests/pooling/routing;
- separate the plain/system intent from the regular counted path.

A possible conceptual form is:

```go
type Dialer struct {
    // state/accounting lifecycle
}

type Scope struct {
    // immutable organization ownership
}

func New(...) *Dialer

func (d *Dialer) ForOrganization(...) (...)
func (s Scope) DialContext(...) (net.Conn, error)
func (s Scope) Wrap(DialFunc) DialFunc
func (d *Dialer) Close()
```

These signatures are **indicative**.

In particular, the design still needs to decide:

- how to express membership;
- how to express counting disabled;
- how to express deleted/uncounted;
- how to integrate listeners and Prometheus;
- whether `Scope` should be a value, an interface, or something else;
- what semantics to give a scope after delete.

## Candidate APIs to remove/move after the migration

To be verified after the consumer migrations:

- `DialWithContext`;
- `WithOrganization` from the connection-level package;
- `PlainDial`;
- `PlainDialWith`;
- `EnableCounting` in its global form;
- the decorators' `nil` fallback.

`DialWithContext` currently has a single production consumer: Lambda.

Do not remove it before the migration.

---

# 23. Proposed direction: organization-aware HTTP package

Working name:

```text
core/internal/orghttp
```

The name is not frozen.

The desired responsibility is:

> **owning HTTP transports/pools and guaranteeing that a counted connection is used by a single organization.**

## 23.1 One owner per configuration domain

The package must be instantiable multiple times, for example:

```text
AWS Lambda configuration
    -> owner #1

application connector HTTP configuration
    -> owner #2

possible S3 configuration
    -> owner #3
```

There does not necessarily have to be a shared global cache.

## 23.2 Two ergonomic modes

### Dynamic/shared logical client

For Lambda or other truly shared clients:

```text
request context
    -> organization
    -> router
    -> per-org transport
```

### Fixed organization facade

For an already bound consumer:

```text
organization in the constructor/boundary
    -> bound facade/transport
```

The consumer must not repeat the organization in the context when it is not needed.

## 23.3 Responsibilities

The package must take care of:

- already configured base transport;
- lazy clone;
- organization -> transport cache;
- synchronization;
- fixed-org connection decorator;
- remove/delete;
- `CloseIdleConnections`;
- shutdown;
- resource safety/membership;
- organization-required mode;
- explicit uncounted mode.

It must know nothing about:

- Krenalis OAuth;
- Lambda business logic;
- S3 settings;
- rate limiting;
- Prometheus internals;
- Snowflake internals.

## 23.4 Dependency direction

The HTTP package must depend on a **narrow connection-accounting abstraction**, not make the dependency on the current global state permanent.

Even if a first implementation internally calls `dialer.DialWith`, the boundary must be designed so that a future state-scoped `Dialer` can be swapped in without rewriting the HTTP consumers.

For this reason, a future API must not be hastily designed as:

```go
New(base *http.Transport, *dialer.Dialer)
```

if a narrower provider/decorator expresses the dependency better.

# 25. Recommended sequence for the future work

The following sequence is recommended, not mandatory.

## Phase 0 — confirm the product scope

Before broadening coverage, decide what "organization network egress" means.

This does not necessarily block the Lambda migration, but it prevents the redesign from assuming goals that have not been agreed upon.

## Phase 1 — define the HTTP boundary

- start from the PoC;
- design the owner per configuration domain;
- define membership and the counted/plain/deleted intents;
- define lifecycle and `Close`;
- define the contract for the supported transports;
- keep dependency inversion toward connection accounting.

## Phase 2 — migrate Lambda

Replace:

```text
DialWithContext
+
DisableKeepAlives
```

with:

```text
single lambda.Client
+
organization-aware HTTP owner
+
per-org pools
+
fixed-org connection accounting
```

Turn the PoC into appropriate production contract/integration tests.

## Phase 3 — integrate/extract the generic HTTP manager

Extract or compose only the low-level layer:

- base transport;
- membership;
- cache;
- clone;
- delete;
- close idle.

Do not drag OAuth, retry, and rate limiting into the common package.

## Phase 4 — redesign the `dialer` lifecycle

Explicitly address:

- instance ownership;
- State listener lifecycle;
- Prometheus lifecycle;
- sequential Cores;
- failed initialization;
- organization recreation.

## Phase 5 — API cleanup

Only after migration and testing:

- verify that `DialWithContext` is dead;
- move/remove `WithOrganization`;
- move `Plain*` into the tests;
- evaluate removing the `nil` fallback;
- rename/refine `Dial`/decorator if it improves the call sites.

# 26. Test contract to preserve in the redesign

Do not lose the properties already demonstrated.

The new code must cover at least:

## HTTP correctness

- known/documented negative control;
- HTTP/1.1;
- HTTP/2;
- keep-alive;
- intra-org reuse;
- absence of cross-org connection reuse;
- per-organization accounting.

## AWS Lambda

- a single `*lambda.Client`;
- real SDK operations against a local/fake endpoint;
- context propagation;
- multiple organizations;
- distinct pools.

## Concurrency

- concurrent first use;
- no duplicate transports;
- `go test -race`;
- I/O outside the cache lock.

## Lifecycle

- lazy creation;
- delete;
- `CloseIdleConnections`;
- in-flight during delete;
- shutdown;
- recreation;
- init failure when relevant.

## Identity / misuse

- missing organization;
- arbitrary unknown ID;
- explicit uncounted;
- deleted cleanup;
- counting disabled.

## Transport contract

- base configuration preserved;
- unsupported `DialTLSContext`/alternate transport rejected or explicitly supported.

# 27. Things NOT to do

Do not replace `DialWith` with `Dial` in consumers that must preserve a configured base dialer.

Do not create a `lambda.Client` per organization just to solve accounting.

Do not use:

```text
shared http.Transport
+
DialWithContext
+
keep-alive
```

for counted multi-organization traffic.

Do not make `DisableKeepAlives` a hidden precondition of the new model.

Do not create a single global HTTP cache for different configurations.

Do not force Snowflake under a request-oriented HTTP router.

Do not replace the Snowflake fork with `Config.Transporter` without an equivalent upstream extension point.

Do not turn naturally fixed-org consumers into context-driven ones without a real benefit.

Do not interpret a missing context as plain in an organization-required client.

Do not create pools from arbitrary, unverified organization IDs.

Do not confuse an arbitrary unknown ID with trusted deleted cleanup.

Do not assume that `RemoveOrganization` automatically invalidates references to already handed-out transports/facades.

Do not assume that moving `dialer`'s global maps into a struct solves the listener and Prometheus lifecycle.

Do not try to solve NATS multiplexing or child-process networking with a `net.Conn` wrapper that does not own the correct attribution boundary.

Do not broaden the product scope of the metric as a side effect of the redesign.

# 30. Final summary

The current implementation can be merged because the production consumers studied satisfy the conditions that make its accounting correct.

In particular, Lambda avoids misattribution by disabling connection reuse.

The future redesign does not arise from `instrumentedConn` being a wrong primitive.

It arises from a more precise understanding of ownership:

```text
connection/pool already owned by an organization
    -> connection-level dialer/decorator

logical HTTP client shared among organizations
    -> separate transport/pool per organization
    -> connection-level accounting below the pool
```

The fundamental property to preserve is:

> **Every counted connection belongs to a single organization for its entire lifetime.**

This property was verified experimentally with:

- HTTP/1.1;
- HTTP/2;
- keep-alive;
- concurrency;
- delete/in-flight;
- real `core/internal/dialer` counters;
- the real AWS Lambda SDK with a single `*lambda.Client`.

Snowflake reinforces the same model: the protocol is HTTP, but the owner is fixed-organization, and the correct point remains the driver's internal dialer.

The main open questions are no longer the feasibility of HTTP pooling, but:

1. the exact scope of the metric;
2. the State/listener/Prometheus lifecycle of the future `dialer`;
3. API/error semantics for membership, deleted, and explicit plain;
4. lifecycle and resource bounds of the HTTP pools;
5. possible coverage of NATS/SMTP/local transformers if included in the product scope.

The future redesign must make ownership a structural property of the system, instead of relying on workarounds such as `DisableKeepAlives` for correctness, without imposing the HTTP router on consumers that are already naturally organization-affine.

items.body:
Part of #4843. TTS module self-review for the Q3 refactor. Line numbers are against main `5c51782c`. Perf numbers come from runs on an H20 (nsys CUDA traces, py-spy at function granularity, a per-step scheduler probe, concurrency sweeps c=1 to c=128); the async-hang findings were verified path-by-path in the code. Happy to share the profiling harness, raw profiles, and the patches mentioned below.

Three problems, in the order we would fix them:

| # | Problem | Kind | Evidence status |
|---|---------|------|-----------------|
| 1 | Async-chunk streaming has no hang safety net; engine failure paths can wedge or over-kill | reliability | every wait traced in code; matches 7 reported issues (1 still open) |
| 2 | `serving_speech.py` adapter migration stopped halfway; 41 model branches remain | maintainability | branch inventory + adapter coverage counted on main |
| 3 | Per-step host work in the worker keeps the GPU ~87% idle under load | performance | nsys + py-spy attribution; fix A/B'd on main, +13% throughput |

---

## Status

Kept here rather than in a comment so it does not scroll away. Every state below was checked against the API on 2026-08-13, not from memory. **Please check this table before starting an item** — four of these were picked up independently and I only noticed after writing a duplicate of one myself (see the note under R1.1).

| Item | State | Where |
|------|-------|-------|
| R1.1 chunk-wait deadline | in review | #3944 (@Ronnie-Rui) — approved, DCO outstanding |
| R1.2 send-failure reporting | in review | #6033 |
| R1.3 prewarm skip fails | in review | #6033 |
| R1.4 timeout validation | in review | #6033 |
| R2.1 non-blocking `sync_q.put` | **open** | — |
| R2.2 per-replica fault isolation | **landed** | #4583 (@ShengleiFu), merged 11 Aug |
| M1 label ladder | **landed** | #4862 (@sphinxkkkbc), merged 4 Jul |
| M2 leaf validators into adapters | **open** | — |
| M3 sampling overrides | in review | #5272 (@sphinxkkkbc) |
| M4 capability metadata | in review | #6138 (@sphinxkkkbc) |
| M5 batch path through adapters | **open** | — |
| M6 delete detection flags | **open** | detection ladder landed in #5682; the flag deletion and CI flip remain |
| W1 hidden-payload opt-out | **open** | patch ready, A/B done, no PR yet |
| W2 prefix-cache step path | **open** | needs worker test coverage first |
| W3 per-step save-path syncs | in review | #5178 (@ShengleiFu) |
| W4 persistent batched buffers | **open** | needs design discussion |
| W5 Code2Wav streaming state | **open** | model-side change |
| K1 static footprint + `required` capture | **open** | — |
| K2 cross-stage memory budget | in review (static half) | #6071 (@Haofan144), framed against #1867 |
| K3 paged KV for TTS | **open, needs scoping** | the live vehicle has moved: RFC #5244 (@asukaqaq-s) and its first implementation #6094 (@zwhzzz0821, scheduler-managed block allocation, 30 files) cover the DiT/diffusion side; RFC #4366 has been quiet since 26 Jun. Neither touches the model-local list KVs this item names |
| K4 memory observability | in review | #5180 (@akshatvishu) |

**On R1.1 and #6033.** #3944 has been open since 28 May and does what R1.1 asks; I wrote the same thing into #6033 on 11 Aug without checking for an open PR against `chunk_transfer_adapter.py`, so that half of #6033 is a duplicate and I am withdrawing it. #3944 is older, has more review on it, and additionally covers the sender-side cleanup path. #6033 will land as R1.2–R1.4 only. Apologies to @Ronnie-Rui for the noise.

If you are picking up an item, a comment here saying so is enough — with 800+ open PRs in this repo, title search alone does not reliably surface in-flight work.

---

## 1. Async-chunk streaming can hang with no safety net

Hangs are the most reported TTS failure class: #142, #322, #1525, #3375, #4463, #4793 (each closed with a point fix), and #3833 is still open. The class keeps coming back because the failures share one root: **the async-chunk path has no timeout net at all**, and several engine failure modes either wedge silently or take down more than they should. We traced every wait on main; the inventory:

| ID | Hang | Trigger | Guard today | Blast radius |
|----|------|---------|-------------|--------------|
| H1 | Serving event loop wedges on a blocking queue put | orchestrator request handler stalls, 256-cap queue fills | none (blocking `sync_q.put`, abort uses the same put) | whole pipeline, incl. `/health` and abort |
| H2 | One dead engine core fail-stops everything | any `StageEngineCoreProc` dies mid-stream | propagation is clean (no silent hang) but promotes to engine-wide `_fatal_error` | whole pipeline |
| H3 | `WAITING_FOR_CHUNK` forever | upstream chunk never arrives (producer crash, dropped terminal chunk, send retries exhausted) | **none** for async-chunk | one request, forever (= open #3833) |
| H4 | `WAITING_FOR_INPUT` (full-payload) | producer never delivers | 600 s net → `FINISHED_ERROR`; **disabled** if `VLLM_OMNI_INPUT_WAIT_TIMEOUT_S<=0` | one request ≤600 s, forever if disabled |
| H5 | Connector get expiry retries silently | transport timeout (mooncake zmq `RCVTIMEO`, yuanrong 1 s poll, shm miss) | metric incremented, no error propagation | feeds H3/H4 |
| H6 | Prewarm silently skipped | stage-0 `prompt_token_ids is None` in async-chunk mode | warning log only | one request, forever |

The details behind the three that matter most:

**H3 — the missing timeout net.** The full-payload path has a 600 s net (`VLLM_OMNI_INPUT_WAIT_TIMEOUT_S`, `omni_scheduler_mixin.py:29`), but it is explicitly scoped away from async-chunk. The scheduler says so:

```python
# core/sched/omni_scheduler_mixin.py:89
Scope: only covers ``input_coordinator`` (full-payload path).
Async-chunk requests park in ``chunk_transfer_adapter`` instead
and are not handled here -- if a similar safety net is needed
for the chunk path, it belongs in the chunk adapter.
```

while the worker-side comment assumes that same net protects it:

```python
# worker/omni_connector_model_runner_mixin.py:374
# Orphaned pending recv entries (e.g. from upstream stage crash)
# are handled by OmniSchedulingCoordinator.collect_timed_out_request_ids()
# which detects wait-time violations.
```

Both cannot be true for async-chunk, and the scheduler comment is the accurate one: `uses_full_payload_input_coordinator` returns False when `async_chunk=True` (`omni_scheduling_coordinator.py:76`), so async-chunk requests park in `WAITING_FOR_CHUNK` via `OmniChunkTransferAdapter` (`distributed/omni_connectors/transfer_adapter/chunk_transfer_adapter.py:23`) and can cycle there forever. The worker's recv thread polls with no per-request deadline (`omni_connector_model_runner_mixin.py:1646-1679`), and when a producer gives up after its 3 send retries ("Giving up on send", `:1732`) the consumer is never told (H5): connector-level expiries just increment a metric and retry. Since async-chunk is the default for the flagship TTS pipelines (`qwen3_tts.yaml: async_chunk: true`), the default streaming path is the unprotected one. A related cleanup: the `connector_get_sleep_s` / `connector_get_max_wait` / `connector_get_max_wait_first_chunk` knobs in every deploy YAML are never read by the shm/chunk path (only a stale comment at `stage_input_processors/qwen3_tts.py:34` mentions them); the real poll intervals are hardcoded in `transfer_adapter/base.py:81,83` (0.1 s idle / 1 ms active). Dead knobs should be wired in or deleted.

**H6 — a request that can never complete, created silently.** If stage-0's `prompt_token_ids` is missing, downstream stages are never pre-registered and the code warns and returns:

```python
# engine/orchestrator.py:1475
if prompt_token_ids is None:
    logger.warning(
        "[Orchestrator] async_chunk prewarm skipped for req=%s: stage0 prompt_token_ids missing",
        request_id,
    )
    return
```

The produced chunks then have no consumer, and the request falls into the H3 no-timeout regime.

**H1 — the whole-pipeline wedge.** The bridge to the orchestrator thread is a bounded janus queue (`_REQUEST_QUEUE_MAXSIZE = 256`, `async_omni_engine.py:67`), and every producer does a blocking put on the sync side from the serving event-loop thread:

```python
# engine/async_omni_engine.py:1285 (add_request; same pattern at :807, :1356, :1408, :1438)
self.request_queue.sync_q.put(msg)
```

If the orchestrator's request handler stalls, the queue fills and the next `put` blocks the event loop itself: no new requests, no `/health`, and, because `abort` uses the same blocking put (`:1408`), no way to abort out of it. The recovery lever is behind the same lock as the failure.

**Verified working, so nobody re-fixes it:** client-disconnect/abort cleanup is complete end to end (orchestrator `request_states`, CFG tracker, bridge states, and the worker's pending-recv table are all released; a stage-0 output arriving after the pop is dropped harmlessly at `orchestrator.py:769`). Engine-core death does not hang anyone: every in-flight and queued request receives a fatal `ErrorMessage` (`orchestrator.py:716-743`, `:1584-1629`). Orchestrator startup is bounded by `stage_init_timeout` plus a deadline on the init future.

### Plan for problem 1

Phase R1, small and independent, each closes a recurrence class:

| Item | Change | Acceptance |
|------|--------|------------|
| R1.1 | `OmniChunkTransferAdapter` gets a `_waiting_since` timeout mirroring `collect_timed_out_request_ids` (`omni_scheduling_coordinator.py:264`), driven from `process_pending_chunks`; on expiry the request fails with a real error | a dropped terminal chunk turns into a client-visible error within the timeout; closes #3833 |
| R1.2 | Producer give-up and recv-deadline expiry propagate as request errors instead of silent retries | killing the upstream stage mid-stream errors the affected requests, not hangs them |
| R1.3 | Async-chunk prewarm skip fails the request explicitly instead of warning | an embeds-only prompt in async-chunk mode returns an error immediately |
| R1.4 | Enforce a floor on `VLLM_OMNI_INPUT_WAIT_TIMEOUT_S` (reject `<=0`) or document `0` as an explicit "no net" opt-in | config cannot silently disable the only full-payload net |

Phase R2, needs design discussion with the engine owners:

| Item | Change | Acceptance |
|------|--------|------------|
| R2.1 | Replace blocking `sync_q.put` with `put_nowait` + backpressure (503) or an executor hop; give `abort` a path that cannot block | a stalled orchestrator degrades to request rejection, `/health` and abort keep working |
| R2.2 | Per-replica fault isolation: fail only requests bound to a dead replica, drain/rebind the rest, instead of engine-wide `_fatal_error` | one replica death does not take down other stages/replicas |

Regression tests to add with R1 (none of these scenarios are covered today): drop the terminal chunk of a stream; kill the upstream stage mid-request; submit an embeds-only prompt in async-chunk mode; fill the request queue with a stalled handler and verify `/health` and abort still respond.

---

## 2. serving_speech.py: the adapter migration stopped halfway

The file is 4,263 lines, one class, 85 methods, and it is the file every TTS model PR touches, which makes it the module's rebase-conflict hotspot. RFC #4327 introduced `tts_adapters/` and its 14 model adapters all implement `build` (all but `covo_audio` also implement `validate`), but the serving file still carries 41 model-type branch clauses across five concerns:

| Concern | Where | Count |
|---------|-------|-------|
| Validation dispatch | `_validate_tts_request` `:1493-1514` | 9 branches |
| Model-label ladder | `:3562-3591` | 14 branches |
| Sampling overrides | `:3602-3716` | ~5 branches |
| Capability loaders (speakers, languages, voices, frame rate, embedding dim, warmup) | `:556-835` and helpers | 11 sites |
| Batch path | `:4163-4228` | bypasses adapters entirely |

The validation dispatcher is still a hand-written ladder:

```python
# serving_speech.py:1498
if self._tts_model_type == "voxtral_tts":
    return self._validate_voxtral_tts_request(request)
if self._tts_model_type == "fish_tts":
    return self._validate_fish_tts_request(request)
if self._tts_model_type == "cosyvoice3":
    return self._validate_cosyvoice3_request(request)
...
```

and the adapters call back INTO that ladder instead of owning their leaf validators, so today the adapter layer adds indirection without removing the dispatch:

```python
# tts_adapters/qwen3_tts.py:41
def validate(self, request: "OpenAICreateSpeechRequest") -> str | None:
    # Go through the shared dispatcher (which routes to
    # _validate_qwen_tts_request for this model-type) rather than the leaf
    # validator directly, matching the pre-adapter qwen3 path.
    return self.ctx.server._validate_tts_request(request)
```

The batch path skips adapters entirely, and says so:

```python
# serving_speech.py:4218
# Batch validation still goes through _validate_tts_request directly
# (not the adapter). ... Routing batch through the adapter (and its
# uploaded-speaker handling) is a follow-up (RFC #4327).
validation_error = self._validate_tts_request(req)
```

Meanwhile the `apply_sampling_overrides` hook exists in `tts_adapters/base.py` but zero adapters implement it, and the 14-way label ladder computes a value the adapter already returns as `PreparedRequest.model_type`.

Three constraints any migration must respect, learned from reading the actual flows:

1. Validation deliberately mutates the request (`task_type`, `voice`, `x_vector_only_mode`, uploaded-speaker `ref_audio/ref_text`) and the prompt builders read the mutated fields. Equivalence checking must diff the post-validation request object, not just the response.
2. Routing `_validate_tts_request` through adapters as-is would recurse (see the qwen3 adapter above). The leaf validators must move into adapters first, then the ladder is deleted.
3. Batch item schemas in `protocol/audio.py` omit fields the single-request schema has (`ref_audio_2`, `ambient_sound`, `speaker_embedding`, `extra_params`). Schema alignment must land before the batch path can route through adapters, or the migration silently changes the batch API surface.

The same copy-paste pattern continues below the serving layer: the codec filter/trim/ref-prepend logic exists in four near-identical copies inside `stage_input_processors/qwen3_tts.py` (inline in `talker2code2wav:61-135`, `talker2code2wav_token_only:401-463`, `talker2code2wav_full_payload:466-555`, plus the async-chunk variant; two carry comments saying "Mirrors the orchestrator-path body"); the talker's scalar decode preprocess duplicates its own batched version (`qwen3_tts_talker.py:728-788` vs `:790-896`); the prompt builder's three task branches share a copy-pasted streaming/non-streaming tail (`prompt_embeds_builder.py:1276-1414`); and the chunk adapter keeps a legacy and an active-stream queue path side by side (`chunk_transfer_adapter.py:556-584` vs `:703-733`). Worth one consolidation pass while the adapter migration is finished.

### Plan for problem 2

Migrate by concern, not by model: each PR is one concern across all models, so every model's e2e stays green per PR and no PR needs a single-model expert. serving_speech has 8 test files (single, batch, stream), the best coverage in this area, so this can start immediately.

| PR | Scope | Deletes | Equivalence oracle |
|----|-------|---------|--------------------|
| M1 | Label ladder → `PreparedRequest.model_type` | 14-branch elif at `:3562` | byte-identical responses; log labels unchanged |
| M2 | Move leaf validators into adapters, route through `adapter.normalize()/validate()` | `_validate_tts_request` + ~10 `_validate_*` methods | byte-identical error strings AND identical post-validation request object per model |
| M3 | Sampling overrides → `apply_sampling_overrides`, preserving today's order (stream-coerce → extra_params → adapter → seed) | inline ladder at `:3602-3716` | identical `SamplingParams` per model incl. qwen3 seed extra_args |
| M4 | Capability metadata → adapter class attributes read through `SpeechServingContext` | 11 loader branch sites | identical `/v1/audio/voices` etc. responses |
| M5 | Batch schema alignment, then batch path through adapters | the `:4218` bypass | batch e2e + schema diff reviewed as an API change |
| M6 | Delete `_is_tts`/`_is_fish_speech`/`_is_cosyvoice3`, `_detect_tts_model_type`, stage-key constants; CI gate flips to error on unmigrated models | the last flags | full suite green |

End state: no model names in the dispatch core; adding a TTS model is one adapter file plus one import.

---

## 3. The worker's per-step host work is where the TTS GPU time actually goes

nsys over a 40 s steady-state window at c=64 shows the GPU executing kernels ~12-13% of wall clock; the pipeline is host-bound, not compute-bound. The step arithmetic makes it concrete: at c=64 the talker averages ~100 ms per decode step (measured tokens/s divided by batch width) while the 1.7B forward itself is worth ~10 ms, and step time nearly doubles from batch 64 to 128 while tokens/s gains only 7%, the signature of per-request Python work inside the step loop rather than GPU compute. Since each step yields 83 ms of audio per request (12 Hz codec), every stream falls behind realtime at c=64 (bench RTF 1.17); cutting step time below ~83 ms is what restores realtime streaming.

Reading the step loop end to end, the per-step host work decomposes into four verified pieces.

**Prefix caching charges per-step CPU rent.** With `enable_prefix_caching: true` (the qwen3_tts default), every decode step runs the mm merge path, which converts all passthrough tensors to CPU:

```python
# core/prefix_cache.py:633
# Then, get everything else (passthrough data); first, convert to CPU
# tensors similarly to the non prefix cached path, ...
mm_cpu = build_mm_cpu(multimodal_outputs=passthrough_mm_data)
```

`_to_cpu` (`utils/mm_outputs.py:93`) is a synchronous copy per tensor, recursing into per-request lists; py-spy puts it at 40.5% of post-fix host samples, with the per-step mm-cache write (`prefix_cache.py:408`) at another 19.2%. The hidden-state copy quoted at the top of this section is gated on `omni_prefix_cache is not None` as well. We priced the whole path with one config flip on main `5c51782c` (same GPU, commit, c=64, `max_num_seqs=64`, 300 requests per arm, all completing with audio):

| stage-0 `enable_prefix_caching` | throughput | mean TTFP | p99 TTFP |
|---|---|---|---|
| true (default) | 45.7 audio-s/s | 1056 ms | 3270 ms |
| false | 53.1 audio-s/s (+16%) | 464 ms (−56%) | 1326 ms |

For this workload prefix caching is net-negative under concurrency: the per-step conversions cost more than the hits save. Two side findings: flipping `enable_prefix_caching: true` on stage 1 crashes at startup (`AssertionError: HybridKVCacheCoordinator requires at least two attention groups`), a config foot-gun worth a validation guard; and the 2-file hidden-payload opt-out we A/B'd earlier (45.7 to 51.7 with caching kept on) overlaps this because both attack the same per-step copy class.

**The stage-1 save path syncs the device every talker step.** In `stage_input_processors/qwen3_tts.py`, `frame.any().item()` (`:144`) and `frame.cpu().tolist()` (`:168`) run per step on the save thread, and each emitted chunk flattens its window with a Python double loop, `torch.tensor([window_frames[f][q] for q in range(nq) for f in range(nf)])` (`:307-310`), roughly 1,500 iterations per chunk.

**The talker's batched decode preprocess still runs a ~50-line Python body per request per step** (`qwen3_tts_talker.py:817-883`: dict merges, per-request tensor slices and casts, per-request update dicts, then two `torch.cat`s over 64 single-row tensors). The batched path already amortizes the embedding lookup (that was a prior optimization); the remaining cost is structural and wants persistent batched GPU buffers for `hidden_states.last` / `trailing_text` indexed by batch slot, instead of per-request dict entries re-gathered every step.

**The vocoder decodes ~4x more than it emits.** Code2Wav decodes the full context+new window, then trims the context off the finished waveform: `start = ctx_frames * upsample; wav = wav[start:end]` (`qwen3_tts_code2wav.py:537-546`). Steady state that is a 97-frame decode for 25 emitted frames. Only ref codes are cached (`_ref_context_cache`, `:106`); no decoder conv/attention state persists across chunks, so the left context is re-synthesized every chunk purely to satisfy the decoder's sliding window (`:162-177`). Two adjacent findings: the cross-request decode grouping and cudagraph batch envelope are inert by default (`_decode_batch_bucket_frames=[]`, `_decode_batch_max_size=0`, `:72`) unless a deploy YAML configures them, and every chunk handoff pays open+flock+mmap+msgpack in both directions because `inline_small_payloads` is unset for TTS (`shm_connector.py:61`).

### Plan for problem 3

| Item | Change | Expected effect | Prerequisite |
|------|--------|-----------------|--------------|
| W1 | Hidden-payload opt-out for qwen3_tts + gate the copy (patch ready, 2 files) | measured: 45.7 to 51.7 audio-s/s, TTFP −55% | none; A/B done |
| W2 | Make the prefix-cache step path pay rent: batch the passthrough conversion into one cat + one D2H per step, extend the existing `gpu_resident_buffer_keys`/deferral mechanism to passthrough keys, or skip CPU conversion when the consumer is the same-GPU next stage | the PC-off flip prices the path at +16% tput / −56% TTFP; W2 should recover that while keeping caching | worker test coverage |
| W3 | Remove per-step syncs in the save path (`:144` `.item()`, `:168` `.cpu().tolist()`) and vectorize the chunk window flatten (`:307-310`) | removes per-step device syncs | none |
| W4 | Persistent batched GPU buffers for `hidden_states.last`/`trailing_text` (replaces the per-request loop at `talker.py:817-883`) | attacks the linear-in-batch step cost directly | design discussion |
| W5 | Streaming decoder state for Code2Wav (carry conv/attention state across chunks instead of re-decoding 72 context frames per chunk) | ~3.9x vocoder FLOP cut steady-state, plus per-chunk latency | model-side change |

Coverage caution before W2: the worker has 5 test files for ~8k lines, and the 2,358-line `omni_connector_model_runner_mixin.py` has a single test. Tests first for anything beyond W1.

---

## 4. Generation stages run with no memory accounting

The AR stage gets vLLM's full memory loop: profile, budget from `gpu_memory_utilization`, paged KV allocation, scheduling against block availability (`GPU KV cache size: 372,336 tokens` on a 0.6B talker at 0.3). Stage 1 (Code2Wav) gets none of it. The model is attention-free from vLLM's point of view, so no KV cache is ever allocated and `gpu_memory_utilization` only gates the initial profile; afterwards nothing is managed.

What actually consumes stage-1 memory sits outside every budget. On an H200-class box the decoder CUDA graph warmup alone moves the torch allocator from 1.85 to 7.56 GiB reserved (9.52 peak) for a model whose weights are 0.5 GiB:

```
# stage-1 boot, cuda_graph_decoder_wrapper.py:360
CUDA Graph warmup complete: 5/5 captured in 1319.9 ms
  (cuda_mem allocated 0.56->0.63 GiB, reserved 1.85->7.56 GiB, max_reserved 1.85->9.52 GiB)
```

Add torch.compile workspaces and the per-request accumulated codec context (up to `max_model_len: 65536` tokens times `max_num_seqs`), none of it admission-controlled. The only self-managing piece on the whole stage is `_ref_context_cache` (entry and byte caps with eviction). The failure modes follow directly: a capture OOM degrades silently (4/5 graphs captured, a WARNING, keeps serving on the slow path), and two stages sharing a GPU are just two static utilization numbers with no arbitration; that 0.5+0.5 OOMs while 0.3+0.3 fits is discovered empirically per box, not guaranteed by anything. Production deployments increasingly expect hard memory accounting and observability from every stage, not only the AR one.

### Plan for problem 4

| Item | Change | Expected effect | Prerequisite |
|------|--------|-----------------|--------------|
| K1 | Measure and document each stage's static footprint (weights + graphs + workspaces) next to its deploy yaml; add a `required` capture mode so graph-capture failure is fail-fast in CI/prod instead of a warning | utilization numbers with a basis; no silent degradation | none |
| K2 | Budget declaration for generation stages: static footprint plus a per-request dynamic ceiling, engine sums per GPU at startup and enforces admission at runtime | removes the cross-stage OOM class | design discussion |
| K3 | Make TTS the second tenant of RFC #4366's paged KV manager: an append-burst lifecycle (connector-fed context, chunked-prefill-with-retention semantics), stage-declared block granularity (`chunk_frames` + `left_context`), sliding-window eviction mapped to the left context. Pilot: Code2Wav decoder KV retention across chunks (subsumes the attention half of W5, removes the ~4x redundant decode), with the write-once conditioning pool replacing `_ref_context_cache`. The model-local list KVs elsewhere in the tree (mimo_audio, minicpmo_4_5, ming_flash_omni talker, and friends) become migration candidates once this lifecycle exists | dynamic memory becomes pool-accounted; admission becomes block availability, same semantics as the AR stage | #4366 Phase 2 scoping with its owners |
| K4 | Observability: per-stage metrics for graph/workspace reservation, pool usage, ref-cache hit rate, accumulated context bytes | ops-grade visibility into stage memory | K1 |

---

## Sequencing

Can start now, independent of each other: R1.1-R1.4 (hang nets), M1-M2 (serving_speech), W1 (patch ready), K1 (measurement + fail-fast capture). Needs tests written first: W2, and any scheduler-adjacent change. Needs engine-owner discussion: R2.1-R2.2, K2. K3 tracks RFC #4366 Phase 2 and should be scoped together with its owners rather than built TTS-side. M-series and R-series touch disjoint files and can run in parallel.

Comments welcome. Raw profiles, the profiling harness, and the patches mentioned above are available on request.

items.body:
**Ready for coding:** yes (2026-10-19). The calls in the table are now checked against the pinned Cloud Director 10.6 `/api` schema files and reference lists of API 39.0 and 39.1, and the pinned CloudAPI 39.2 file.

## Goal

An agent can list provider VDCs, read organisation VDCs, and create, change and delete organisation VDCs — each change with approval.

## Why

- Creating the organisation VDC is the second step of tenant onboarding.
- The tool comparison (govc, PowerCLI, Terraform, Ansible, the vendor SDKs) marks these as the usual work: Manage provider VDCs; Manage organization VDCs.

## What to build

| Operation (proposed id) | What it does | Vendor call (service, method, path) | Risk | Versions |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `vcd.pvdc.list` | Provider VDCs: vCenter, resource pools, storage policies, state. | CloudAPI `GET /cloudapi/1.0.0/providerVdcs` | read | 10.6 |
| `vcd.vdc.get` | One organisation VDC: allocation model, limits, use, storage policies, network pool. | CloudAPI `GET /cloudapi/1.0.0/vdcs/{orgVdcId}` | read | 10.6 |
| `vcd.vdc.create` | Create an organisation VDC (tenant onboarding, step 2). | `/api` `POST /api/admin/org/{id}/vdcsparams` | change (dangerous) | 10.6 |
| `vcd.vdc.update` | Change the limits or storage policies of an organisation VDC. | `/api` `PUT /api/admin/vdc/{id}`, `POST /api/admin/vdc/{id}/vdcStorageProfiles`, `PUT /api/admin/vdcStorageProfile/{id}` | change (dangerous) | 10.6 |
| `vcd.vdc.delete` | Delete an empty organisation VDC. | `/api` `POST /api/admin/vdc/{id}/action/disable` then `DELETE /api/admin/vdc/{id}` | change (destructive) | 10.6 |
| `vcd.pvdc.update` | Add or remove resource pools and storage policies of a provider VDC. | REST `POST /api/admin/extension/providervdc/{id}/action/updateResourcePools`, REST `POST /api/admin/extension/providervdc/{id}/storageProfiles` | change (dangerous) | 10.6 |

**Risk and approval (how MEHO works today).** A **read** is `safe` and runs at once. Every **change** sets `requires_approval: true` and the safety level in the table.

- A person's call waits in the approval queue until a second person approves it (MEHO refuses self-approval by default). A `destructive` change always waits, even without the flag.
- An agent's call: `caution` waits for approval. `dangerous` is refused unless the agent holds a grant for it; with a grant it waits for approval. `destructive` is always refused for an agent, even with a grant (`auth/permissions.py`). A person runs it instead.
- A `destructive` change needs a preview first. The person calls `preview_operation` with the same inputs, then `call_operation` with the `preview_hash` it returned. The preview says which object changes, what else is affected and what cannot be undone (the `blast_radius` block, filled by the operation's preview builder).

**Versions** says where the call exists: the connector generations that register it (for example `8.0, 9.x`), or a first version (for example `9.1+`: 9.1 and newer only). The proposed ids follow the connector's naming pattern; keep that pattern if you must change an id. The vendor call column names the service and the exact method or path. If a call is wrong, fix the call and this table, not the test.

**Versions.** Register on `vcd-rest-10.6` (Cloud Director 10.6.x, API version 39). Use CloudAPI (`/cloudapi`) where it has the object, and the older `/api` where it does not. Cloud Director 10.5 is not part of this program (a version exception).

## Acceptance criteria

### Implemented (this pull request)

- [ ] Each operation in the table is a typed operation (written by hand in MEHO code). It works on a fresh install, with no spec ingest.
- [ ] On each of these versions — Cloud Director 10.6 — each operation does what the table says where its **Versions** column includes that version, and stops early with the version message where it does not. The docs table copies the Versions column.
- [ ] Each operation works on Cloud Director 10.6.
- [ ] Every change has `requires_approval: true` and the safety level in the table; every read is `safe`. A test checks both fields for each operation in the table.
- [ ] Each `destructive` change has a preview builder (`register_preview_builder` in `operations/_preview.py`). It reads the object first and fills the `blast_radius` block: `object`, `children` (what else is affected) and `irreversibility` (what cannot be undone). It refuses when the object does not exist. Tests cover both cases, and one test shows the call is refused without a matching `preview_hash`.
- [ ] No result contains a password, token, private key or licence key in clear text. An input that is a secret is a Vault reference (`secret_ref`), never the value.
- [ ] Each operation has: a one-line summary; a description; a description on every parameter field, also nested ones; `enum` where a field has fixed values; `oneOf` or `anyOf` where the rule is "either A or B"; a response schema that names the main fields; `llm_instructions` with `when_to_call`, `output_shape` and `next_step` (and `preconditions` for a change); and one example call under `examples` in the parameter schema.
- [ ] A list comes back as a flat list of rows. Then MEHO stores a long list behind a link (a result handle), and the agent reads it with `result_query`.
- [ ] Examples use neutral placeholders such as `<vm-name>` or `<cluster-id>`, never values that look real, so a model does not copy them as real choices (the lesson of #4111).
- [ ] The summary is one line and the description stays short (about 300 characters at most); longer guidance goes into `llm_instructions`, so search answers stay small (the aim of #4112).
- [ ] Each group text (`when_to_use`) says in plain words which reads and changes the group holds. It makes no claim about the safety of the whole group.
- [ ] `docs/codebase/connectors-vcd.md` lists the new operations: what each one does, what it returns, and which versions have it. `docs-site/reference/connectors.md` is regenerated.
- [ ] The full unit test suite passes.

### Checked against vendor files (this pull request, in CI)

- [ ] The reconcile guard checks every vendor call in the table: CloudAPI paths are checked against the cell-served CloudAPI file on the spec shelf (API 39.2, a Swagger 2.0 file: write a small path extractor, as the reconcile standard allows); `/api` paths go into the manifest pin with the reference link.
- [ ] If a pinned file is new to CI, `.github/workflows/ci.yml` gets its folder in the spec-shelf sparse checkout and its main file in the required-file list of the same job. Then CI fails when the file is missing, instead of skipping the lane.
- [ ] The operation-contract CI check passes and lists no new gap for these operations.

### Proved live (a separate lab proof, not this pull request)

- Not in this Task. A separate lab proof runs every operation in the table on Cloud Director 10.6 and records pass, fail or "not available on this version", with the date. This Task needs no lab and no live system.

## How to test without a live target

1. Write small saved responses (fixtures) by hand from the vendor API reference. Use made-up names and ids, never real ones.
2. Mock HTTP with `respx`, like `tests/test_connectors_vcd_typed_reads.py` does.
3. For each change: one test that it waits for approval, one test of the success path, and one test of a vendor error (the error text reaches the answer).
4. Reconcile guard (a CI test that checks each vendor path against the pinned API file): run `MEHO_CONSUMER_DOCS_ROOT=<spec shelf>/docs uv run pytest tests/test_connectors_vcd_spec_reconcile.py`. Without the shelf the lane skips on your machine; CI runs it.
5. Regenerate the reference page: `cd backend && uv run python scripts/generate_reference_docs.py`.
6. Run everything, without stopping at the first failure: `cd backend && uv run pytest tests/ -q -n auto`, then `uv run ruff check src/ tests/`, `uv run ruff format --check src/ tests/` and `uv run mypy src/`.

## Scope

- In: the six operations above.
- Out: provider VDC create (setup work).

## Rules

- This is a public repository. Do not write lab names, host names, IP addresses, customer names or internal ticket names into code, tests, fixtures, commits or the pull request.
- Do not edit `CHANGELOG.md`. The release pull request adds the line.

## Depends on

This Task waits for these issues:

Depends-on: #4519
Depends-on: #4315

labels.name: needs-decision
labels.description: Blocked on a call from Josh

items.body:
Raised by Josh 2026-09-19 (#admin), for deliberate planning (NOT a rush - his words: "not saying hey rush and go do that").

JOSH'S THESIS: the Windows and Mac clients will DIVERGE as each specializes for its OS (they get more different, not more alike). So sharing should be "copy the good idea and reimplement it your way," not "share the same code." A shared repo fights that trajectory; a separate Windows repo (a) matches the divergence, (b) prevents Mac/Windows agent card-confusion - critical as Homer brings more Windows agents in (they would risk grabbing Mac cards, and vice versa).

SPLINTER UPDATED POSITION: agreed. My earlier "don't fork the shared code" assumed the platforms should stay in sync; Josh's point is they deliberately won't. With intentional divergence, a separate Windows repo is the right structure, and the label+picker band-aid (#3290) does not scale past a few agents.

PLAN NEEDED (scope WITH Homer, who owns the Windows build + knows what is actually Windows-specific):
- The SEAM: what MOVES to the new Windows repo, what (if anything) stays genuinely shared - the deep engine (agent management, provider sessions, the board protocol) is the big common surface today - vs copied-and-reimplemented per Josh's model.
- The Windows-agent CARD POOL: how Homer's agents get only Windows cards and Mac agents only Mac cards (clean repo boundary replaces the label filter).
- Migration steps + what breaks during the cutover.

Splinter to bring Josh a concrete migration plan for his GO before execution. Interim protection: #3290 (Mac pickers skip the `windows` label) covers the current few-agent reality while the split is planned.

# Chairman outcome and bounded ownership

Operation/root: `grok-secretary-access-visibility-20261105-c4`. Parent architecture: #983 / WS:EXECUTIVE-CAPACITY-FABRIC. Current Chairman instruction (2026-11-05): census Subagent Fabric and Hermes/BYOK surfaces, then design and implement Secretary access/full visibility so GB1 becomes Meta-CEO, Secretary 2 remains Secretary, and both share a durable economical watcher/worker team.

**Exclusive boundary:** Y7 Elevate Retail `Audit BYOK Harness System` owns Hermes/BYOK harness forward motion. This project owns only the consumer access/visibility layer and integration seams. No changes to Y7's runtime, BYOK credentials, isolation, installation or deployment carriers (#1966, #2080 and original #1841). Existing application-Fabric writers under #983 remain separate.

Protected procedure/source pin: Mastermind `531bd22b03ffac002221b6a75fe70be70e13f417`, Skillpack v1.0.1, bootstrap major 1. Source workspace uses existing mmx-workspace owner and branch `sol/web-grok-secretary-access-visibility-20261105-c4`. Initial acquisition reported unqualified; original same-operation publish/status and workspace CLI readback reconciled it to clean registered workspace at the exact base, no remote branch and no source edit.

## Initial plan (editorial; no runtime admission)

- P1 — Census incumbent role-authenticated ingress, Fabric projections/results, return/wake/subscription owners, Secretary local access and Y7 interfaces. Output: source-linked capability map, exact seams and missing live evidence.
- P2 — Freeze and implement the smallest useful consumer vertical: shared team visibility, bounded changes/attention and safe intent/control delegation through existing owners. GB1/Secretary 2 use separate authenticated principals; team scope cannot come from model claims. No new scheduler, queue, worker/result registry, identity, retry, auth or usage store.
- P3 — Qualify stale/foreign scope, restart/unknown effects, bounded output and original-parent consumption; publish source with focused tests/CI and a Cursor integration contract. Runtime adoption only through incumbent owners; preserve actual security/release holds.
- P4 — Prove the real GB1 + Secretary 2 journey: both observe one canonical team; permitted create/steer reaches admitted child; meaningful result returns to exact action owner; unchanged monitoring produces no reasoning turns. Week-long endurance and measured token savings remain unproven until observed.

## Initial facts

Fabric MCP capabilities are readable: adapter available, manual strict routing available, worker admission/start UNPROBED, native_parent_wake=false, background_execution=false, controller tracking process-generation-only/not restart-persistent. Executive reader returned backend_unavailable before sending its read. Studio workspace discovery and registered workspace readback work; aggregate fleet status returned OWNER_RESULT_INVALID (not proof of a general outage). GitHub/Slack read capability verified; Grok Secretary U0BTCHX8HMF resolves to groksecretary@mastermind-x.com.

## Acceptance and falsifiers

A published adapter or green CI alone is not completion. Preserve actual Job/Attempt/root/parent identity, exact effect reconciliation, honest freshness/coverage/unknowns, two-principal authorization and one current action owner. Consumer must not choose provider credentials/accounts/hosts or revive a terminal/uncertain operation. Prove useful real result consumption and token economy with evidence, not configured polling intervals or estimated savings.

No live enrollment, role replacement, provider spend, always-on service or watcher has been started by this project. Checkpoints remain here and in the source plan/PR; Slack is transport.

items.title: [Help Wanted] vLLM Router 2026 Roadmap

labels.name: High Priority
labels.description: issues with high priority and expected to be triaged asap

labels.name: omni-modality
