items.title: RFC: K3s backend for persistent T3 hosting and isolated agent workers
items.body:
<!-- oss-factory:v1
{"id":"20261028-t3code-k3s-adapter-001","kind":"work_order","project":"t3code","from":"chatgpt","to":["factory"],"status":"queued","civ":{"city_id":"oss:t3code"},"dedupe_key":"t3code-k3s-environment-worker-adapter-v1"}
-->

## Goal
Make **self-hosted K3s a practical execution backend for T3 Code**, using T3's existing remote-environment and delegation architecture. One persistent T3 control environment should be able to launch, monitor, resume, cancel, and clean up isolated agent environments on a local K3s cluster, with web/desktop/mobile clients staying usable.

**Scope / updated authorization (October 28, 2026):** User explicitly authorized exactly one upstream design issue, [pingdotgg/t3code#26535](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/issues/26535), which maintainers converted to an Ideas discussion on 2026-10-28; the original issue remains a read-only provenance link. All continuing engineering and coordination remain **downstream in `kvnloo/t3code`**; no additional upstream issues, PRs, comments, default-branch writes or merges without a new human authorization. Preserve contributor credit. This is a capability proposal, **not** a claim of native K3s support.

## Problem / distinctions
There are two independent questions to validate:

1. **Host T3 on K3s:** headless server, stable public/private endpoint, persistence, pairing/auth, upgrades and restart recovery.
2. **Use K3s for worker execution:** provision a separate sandbox/T3 environment per approved task, route a remote agent invocation to it, retain task state, and safely reclaim resources.

Packaging a container does **not** automatically provide scheduling; T3 remote delegation does **not** automatically create or manage pods.

## Relevant upstream work (recheck exact heads/status before coding)
- [Remote delegation PR #16719](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/pull/16719) merged **into feature branch `t3code/peer/links-ui` on Oct 27**, not proof of availability on `main` or in a stable release. Use only after checking integration.
- [Remote launch recovery #17051](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/issues/17051) documents a record-before-launch durability gap; [PR #20937](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/pull/20937) closed unmerged on Oct 27.
- [External sandbox broker #14793](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/issues/14793) and [managed workers #14620](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/issues/14620) describe nearby approaches. Their issue dispositions do not establish that provisioning shipped.
- Docker/Kubernetes-oriented container PRs [#5287](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/pull/5287) and [#5284](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/pull/5284) closed unmerged; avoid repeating broad auth/UI changes.
- [Pairing/public URL #13582](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/issues/13582#issuecomment-6034644422) includes a Kubernetes ingress/pod-IP use case.
- [Container host identity #11849](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/issues/11849) remains relevant; avoid per-restart identity drift. [Nested rootless kind/Podman issue #21730](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/issues/21730) is related but separate; [PR #21700](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/pull/21700) closed unmerged as of Oct 28.
- Existing factory [kind → K3s CPU Job pilot](https://github.com/kvnloo/oss-factory/issues/127) is about verified-work jobs, not T3 remote-environment lifecycle. Reuse evidence/fixtures if useful; do not create a second scheduler.

## Proposed minimal architecture
```text
Web / Desktop / Mobile
         |
persistent T3 owner (threads, approvals, durable orchestration)
         |
optional external K3s environment broker (idempotent request/lease)
         |
K3s API --> per-task isolated T3 server + workspace/PVC + agent runtime
         |
connected environment / scoped remote delegation
         |
result, logs, status, artifacts --> owning T3 thread
```

- **Owner authority stays singular.** No distributed SQLite, shared writable checkout, or cross-pod takeover of an owning thread.
- **External adapter first.** Implement a narrow K3s broker/sidecar and declarative manifests before changing core T3 contracts/UI. Avoid a second scheduler and unnecessary hosted-cloud dependencies.
- **Task identity is durable.** Stable idempotency key, exact repo/commit/branch, pod/environment ID, TTL, cancellation/restart states and recovered receipts. Never treat pod completion alone as an accepted agent result.
- **Security by default.** Namespace/service-account/RBAC least privilege; pod security, network policies and CPU/RAM/GPU limits; scoped Git/provider credentials; no public ingress by default; explicit pairing/approval. Do not log secrets.
- **Data lifecycle.** Separate owner state from per-task workspace/PVC. Define stop/resume/archive/delete explicitly. Cancellation and idle cleanup must not delete user work without consent.
- **Performance.** No extra work when disabled, bounded polling/WS updates, report cold-start/provisioning latency and resource overhead. Local-only K3s must work without cloud GPUs.

## Acceptance / staged proof
- [ ] **Inventory:** check current upstream `main` and relevant feature branches; document existing remote/server, container, pairing and authentication capabilities, blockers and non-goals with links.
- [ ] **P0 — hosting:** on a real single-node local K3s cluster, deploy a persistent headless T3 server with a stable reachable endpoint and storage; pair a client; restart/upgrade the pod and verify thread/state survives. Provide manifests and rollback instructions. Record exact image SHA/tag, K3s version and host.
- [ ] **P1 — one worker:** from the owning T3 environment, submit an approved test task against a pinned repo revision; provision exactly one isolated K3s worker; connect/execute; deliver its actual result to the owner; show status from at least web or mobile.
- [ ] **Failure tests:** duplicate request, lost launch response, pod eviction/restart, owner restart, unreachable worker, cancel, expired lease and credential revocation each have defined recovery and no duplicate accepted completion.
- [ ] **Isolation:** demonstrate resource caps, scoped auth/network access, no secret leakage in logs, and no shared mutable owner DB/workspace.
- [ ] **Evidence:** capture exact-head checks, focused tests, runtime transcripts, observed provisioning/cold-start and cleanup times, remaining unsupported modes and unresolved upstream dependencies.

## Execution / return
1. Start with **read-only architecture and overlap audit**; classify any dependency blocked by unmerged/rebased upstream work.
2. Make the smallest independently testable fork-only implementation slice, ideally out-of-tree K3s adapter/manifests before core UI changes.
3. Report tests and artifacts **on this issue**, with `PASS / FAIL / NOT RUN`, tested commit and exact K3s environment. Keep any eventual fork PR separate and in draft; do not merge or post upstream.
4. Add only proven, qualified implementation to the existing [T3Code promotion queue #42](https://github.com/kvnloo/t3code/issues/42). A READY classification is not upstream authorization.

---

## Expansion: PAIR-informed inference and private multi-host mesh (2026-10-28)

**Human objective:** expand this program with prior NVIDIA **Personal AI Router (PAIR)**, heterogeneous/local GPU affinity and eventually scale a bounded T3/K3s worker fabric across **Tailscale or other authenticated private VPNs**. This is **deferred roadmap scope**; it does not relax the P0/P1 proof gates or authorize new upstream writes, live deployment, host changes or competing task schedulers. Keep Draft PR [#46](https://github.com/kvnloo/t3code/pull/46) strictly P0.

### Ownership boundaries and minimal interfaces

```text
T3 owner (task state, approvals, delegation, result verification)
       |
optional K3s environment broker (idempotent provision/lease/delete)
       |
private address + attested T3 environment identity + user-approved /mcp peer link
       |
T3 worker environments on approved hosts or independent K3s clusters
       | (optional; inference only)
PAIR-compatible inference gateway -> eligible model-serving host
       |
verified owner result + bounded telemetry -> existing evaluation/policy systems
```

- **T3 remains the only agent/task authority**; T3's saved client connection, peer-link OAuth grant and runtime provisioning lease are three distinct identities/authorizations.
- **K3s/Kubernetes** schedules pods; do not stretch one K3s control plane across intermittent WAN hosts by default. Begin with separate clusters and expose only approved workloads/endpoints across the private network. No Karmada/Nomad/new scheduler in the baseline.
- **PAIR** routes *independent inference requests* to one compatible serving node (model inventory, available GPU/RAM, workload, observed affinity); it is not a K3s worker scheduler and does not pool 12 GB + 8 GB into 20 GB or shard a live model across hosts. It must be optional: preserve the existing provider endpoint when disabled.
- **Network** is a replaceable *transport*: a private HTTPS endpoint, stable T3 environment ID, verified peer identity, approval and authorization boundaries. Tailscale Kubernetes Operator ingress/egress is the first supported candidate. Later independently assess Headscale + Tailscale clients, NetBird, and configured WireGuard/other private VPN routes; do not assume Tailscale Operator OAuth/Ingress automatically works with those replacements. Manual DNS/endpoint discovery is acceptable; multicast is not assumed. No public Funnel or unrestricted cluster API.
- **Isolation and learning** remain separate: no provider secrets in model/worker telemetry; the overlay network alone does not authorize a T3 peer or PAIR node; no automatic scaling/placement changes without deterministic budget/security limits and human opt-in.

### P2 — multi-host/private-network expansion (after verified P0 and P1)

- [ ] Test two explicitly approved independent environments over LAN then tailnet, then two independent K3s clusters via Tailscale Operator cross-cluster Service ingress/egress (stable private FQDN, HTTPS, no exposed kube API). Record packet route (direct vs relay), DNS behavior, RTT, throughput, handshake/reconnect and negative ACL proof. Do not mistake connected for authorized.
- [ ] Define a minimal VPN-neutral `PrivateEnvironmentEndpoint` record: `environmentId`, authenticated `httpsOrigin`, identity verification, transport label, tested reachability status, last probe and lease reference. Keep all credentials out of record, Git and logs.
- [ ] Demonstrate remote owner->worker link/delegation with parent/worker restarts, duplicate request, route churn, approval revocation, offline/disconnected cluster, cancellation, exact result/receipt identity and no duplicate accepted completion. No automatic enrollment of transient workers in client auto-balance.
- [ ] Compare private options only on real supported setups (Tailscale first; Headscale/NetBird/WireGuard after matching gateway/identity capabilities are verified). Leave unsupported transport `NOT RUN`, not implicitly compatible.

### P3 — PAIR-informed inference gateway (separate from task placement)

- [ ] Inventory `kvnloo/Personal-AI-Router` and the official [NVIDIA/Personal-AI-Router](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Personal-AI-Router), read PAIR's current runtime/engine and actual gateway/protocol capabilities, and find a compatible T3-controlled harness endpoint (e.g. explicitly configured OpenAI-compatible model gateway if supported). Never assume all T3 harnesses accept a PAIR endpoint.
- [ ] Explicitly account for **PAIR's existing cross-VPN discovery limitations**: [#85](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Personal-AI-Router/issues/85), [#91](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Personal-AI-Router/issues/91), [#92](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Personal-AI-Router/issues/92); PAIR uses mDNS on LAN and must have a *verified* unicast/manual-node or fixed implementation for VPN-only peers. [Origin PR #10](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Personal-AI-Router/pull/10) proposes address-based overlay support but was still open in this review. No claim it shipped.
- [ ] Reuse the already researched node/engine/model eligibility, warm-model affinity, GPU class/VRAM headroom, cold-start penalty, current queue and tailnet RTT; route each independent request to a single eligible node, never pool VRAM or interrupt/reschedule a streaming response.
- [ ] Verify which backend *actually* served a request. Previous downstream PAIR [PR #2](https://github.com/kvnloo/Personal-AI-Router/pull/2) proposes authoritative `X-PAIR-Served-By` after failover but is closed/unmerged; do **not** rely on this header without confirming upstream behavior. Collect verified scheduler/engine receipts or mark attribution unproven.
- [ ] Compare explicit local-only baseline against two-node eligible routing using p50/p95 TTFT, tokens/sec, p95 tail latency, model load/cold start, tokens/J or watt-hours when available, GPU memory/power, request failures, and network/relay overhead. Record tested model, engine, node, network and exact versions. Compare aggregate throughput and utilization, not claim faster single-request inference.

### P3b — optional KAI GPU fractioning (gated, not part of P0/P1)

**Decision: HOLD / read-only compatibility research until a measured need exists.** GPU fractioning is a node-level enforcement adapter for **KAI-assigned, same-physical-GPU fractions**, not a T3 placement system, PAIR model router, cross-host memory pool, or new scheduler. Keep existing CPU-only P0 and single-worker P1 manifests unchanged; do not install the operator, touch the NVIDIA driver/container runtime, evict active GPU tenants, or create GPU pods on a working host without a separate explicit owner-approved rollback/maintenance plan.

- **Ownership and contract:** T3 owns the user-approved task/peer link and verified result; z0intelligence validates semantic eligibility and policies; Kerdoios may offer an opt-in bounded capacity ranking; Kubernetes/Kueue owns resource admission; **KAI Scheduler chooses the GPU and fractional memory allocation**; **`gpu-fractioning`** manages node NRI/`fractiond` and MPS/`mpsd` memory enforcement plus `metricsd` per-pod observation; PAIR routes *independent* inference calls only. Existing `z0.capacity.snapshot.v1` [z0 #131](https://github.com/kvnloo/z0intelligence/issues/131), [#133](https://github.com/kvnloo/z0intelligence/issues/133), [#134](https://github.com/kvnloo/z0intelligence/issues/134) is the optional **read-only** capacity bridge; `unknown` is not zero and a capacity offer is not runtime authorization.
- **Compatibility gates (verify live, do not assume):** [current source at `dbf2d4e`](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/gpu-fractioning/blob/dbf2d4e2de66812a5ecfe58400e23859251ee270/README.md) requires Kubernetes >=1.28; containerd >=2.0 with NRI enabled (or supported CRI-O); NVIDIA GPU Operator >=26.7.0, toolkit >=1.20.1, device plugin >=0.20.1, and **NVIDIA driver r615+ / CUDA 13.4**. GPU Operator's NRI mode changes RuntimeClass and requires management CDI namespace allowlisting. Check actual K3s-bundled containerd/CRI/NRI, driver, toolkit, device-plugin versions and GPU support on **each** node before even drafting an install command. The working RTX 3080 Ti 12 GB and RTX 2080 Super 8 GB do **not** form one 20 GB VRAM pool, and do not have MIG; a fractional share is within an individual compatible physical GPU.
- **Separate two generations:** existing GPU **memory** fractions with `time-slicing` or `sm-sharing` are distinct from planned guaranteed **compute** fraction requests/ceilings. The latter is [KAI #2191](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/KAI-Scheduler/issues/2191), [#2192](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/KAI-Scheduler/issues/2192), [gpu-fractioning #157](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/gpu-fractioning/issues/157) and [#163](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/gpu-fractioning/issues/163), **Alpha / driver r620+ / CUDA 13.5**, not assumed production-ready or usable on r615 alone.
- **Known live upstream risks to review before any real fractioning canary:** [#165](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/gpu-fractioning/issues/165) documents stale container/metrics mapping after reconnect; [PR #166](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/gpu-fractioning/pull/166) has a focused unmerged patch. [#167](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/gpu-fractioning/issues/167) documents `GpuFractioningConfig` Helm hook upgrade/uninstall lifecycle pitfalls. Treat "pod Ready" and nonzero metric output as insufficient proof of actual memory enforcement. Verify driver/MPS failures, hard memory cap/OOM, container restart, device placement, metrics cleanup, driver upgrade/drain and uninstall/rollback on an isolated disposable GPU test host before promotion.
- **Experiment path:** (A) read-only version/physical GPU probe and frozen baseline; (B) ordinary exclusive whole-GPU K3s Job on one eligible node, with normal provider throughput/performance and no user-impact regression; (C) on a separate approved isolated GPU test node, **two fixed, safe, low-memory test pods on the same GPU** with KAI-issued fraction annotations, driver/NRI limits, instrumented OOM negative control and independent metrics; (D) only if worthwhile, compare whole-GPU vs time-slicing vs sm-sharing on verified useful work per GPU-second, prefill/decode p50/p95, model memory, watts, crash/error rate, and tailnet cost. Guard all writes and changes behind human approval. No new CRD or second cluster scheduler.
- **Attention gate:** actively research prereqs and upstream bug resolution now, but **no GPU fractioning PR or live deployment as part of this T3 lane until P0 live storage/route acceptance, P1 one isolated worker, and exclusive GPU baseline each pass**. Keep source-specific issues/PRs in their existing repos; consolidate cross-project status in this issue and keep the upstream T3 Ideas discussion high-level.

### P4 — optional verified adaptive placement (not in T3 core)

- [ ] Reuse the existing **Evolution Lab -> z0evals -> z0intelligence -> Kerdoios -> Kueue/KAI/KEDA** governance from prior ABAB research. Learn only bounded legal actions (route, warm/cold policy, queue/replicas/placement hints) after deterministic eligibility/security and quota checks. Preserve Kueue admission, KAI GPU placement and KEDA elasticity; never add a second privileged learning scheduler to T3.
- [ ] Require offline replay -> shadow -> limited canary -> separately authorized promotion, exact experimental lineage, independent acceptance and fail-safe rollback. Do not train weights or automate new infrastructure during the P0 pilot.

## References — consolidated evidence and ownership index (2026-10-28)

This section is the **single** cross-project reference index for this T3/K3s proposal. The linked upstream idea is for architecture discussion, not a second execution queue. Keep detailed implementation/measurements in their original owning repositories. Source links denote the *current published design or reported defect*, not confirmation that the related cluster has been tested.

### 1. T3 execution and discussion

- [T3 Code K3s work order, this issue #45](https://github.com/kvnloo/t3code/issues/45) — **canonical intent, gates, and dependency/attention ledger**; [Draft PR #46](https://github.com/kvnloo/t3code/pull/46) — CPU-only, persistent T3 P0 deployment and restart-identity acceptance, **LIVE K3s / Tailscale NOT RUN** (last inspected head `8da283b04954a02b57c1b0234e27032731fa7fb2`; re-read before next worker action).
- [T3 upstream issue #26535](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/issues/26535) — converted by maintainer to an **Ideas discussion** on October 28; original issue is locked, direct discussion URL not supplied by the issue REST view. No upstream PR approval; treat converted thread as a concise design question, **not** another progress-report destination.
- [T3 remote architecture](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/blob/main/docs/internals/remote.md) + [remote access](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/blob/main/docs/user/remote-access.md) — stable environment identity, private routes, peer-link OAuth and delegated tasks; [#9895](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/pull/9895) — existing connected-machine load balancing; [#16719](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/pull/16719) — remote delegation; [#17051](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/issues/17051) — record-first launch recovery still needs independently validated durability; [#15350](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/pull/15350) — **separate** same-host Docker sandbox implementation, avoid overlap.

### 2. Existing z0 / fleet planning (not a second scheduler)

- [z0intelligence #131](https://github.com/kvnloo/z0intelligence/issues/131) — canonical federated capacity plane: typed `CapabilityDemand -> CapacityOffer -> PlacementLease`; semantic eligibility in z0, capacity economics in Kerdoios, actual execution/admission in existing runtimes. [Fleet migration research comment](https://github.com/kvnloo/z0intelligence/issues/131#issuecomment-6356821555) explicitly rejects fleet-wide GPU/cluster migration without host safety and runtime evidence (its historic fleet report is owner-supplied, not independently re-probed).
- [z0 #133](https://github.com/kvnloo/z0intelligence/issues/133) / [#134](https://github.com/kvnloo/z0intelligence/issues/134) — read-only `z0.capacity.snapshot.v1` hardware, Tern and Kerdoios inputs, stable identities and sticky/nonmigratable active sessions; [Kerdoios #50](https://github.com/kvnloo/kerdoios/issues/50) — hardware-aware local SLM resource placement; [Kerdoios #51](https://github.com/kvnloo/kerdoios/issues/51) — quota/offer economics.
- [`.files` #23](https://github.com/kvnloo/.files/issues/23) — actual explicit K3s host/cluster onboarding, **CPU-first and GPU-fractioning deferred**, no automatic host/driver edits; [OSS Factory #127](https://github.com/kvnloo/oss-factory/issues/127) / [Draft #128](https://github.com/kvnloo/oss-factory/pull/128) — existing bounded K8s Job renderer and offline safety tests, **live kind/K3s not independently proven**. Reuse fixtures, not scheduling authority.

### 3. GPU fractioning, KAI and release risks

- [kai-scheduler/gpu-fractioning](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/gpu-fractioning) — authoritative current [README @ `dbf2d4e`](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/gpu-fractioning/blob/dbf2d4e2de66812a5ecfe58400e23859251ee270/README.md) for NRI/MPS/metricsd, memory annotations, runtime prerequisites and CDI caveats; [existing downstream fork](https://github.com/kvnloo/gpu-fractioning) — research/patch coordination if a concrete, nonduplicated fix emerges, not another T3 scheduler.
- [KAI Scheduler](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/KAI-Scheduler) allocates fractional devices; [KAI #2191](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/KAI-Scheduler/issues/2191) / [#2192](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/KAI-Scheduler/issues/2192) — compute-fraction feature/design, distinct from memory fraction. [GPU Fractioning #157](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/gpu-fractioning/issues/157) / [#163](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/gpu-fractioning/issues/163) — node-side alpha r620+ compute fraction requirements.
- [GPU Fractioning #165](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/gpu-fractioning/issues/165) / [PR #166](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/gpu-fractioning/pull/166) — stale-container-mapping bug/unmerged patch; [#167](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/gpu-fractioning/issues/167) — default CR Helm hook lifecycle issue. Review existing owners and current heads before discussing fixes; do not claim those are resolved or independently measured.
- [NVIDIA GPU Operator](https://github.com/NVIDIA/gpu-operator), [NVIDIA container toolkit](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-toolkit), [NVIDIA device plugin](https://github.com/NVIDIA/k8s-device-plugin) — prereqs: Kubernetes >=1.28, containerd >=2.0 with NRI, GPU Operator >=26.7.0, toolkit >=1.20.1, device plugin >=0.20.1, driver r615+ for memory fractions; compute-fraction prototype targets r620+. **No host/runtime upgrade was made or approved.**

### 4. Private-network and inference separation

- [Tailscale Kubernetes Operator](https://tailscale.com/docs/kubernetes-operator/) — first private-cluster ingress/egress candidate; [service mirroring](https://tailscale.com/docs/kubernetes-operator/ingress/multi-cluster-service-mirroring) for future independent K3s clusters. [Headscale](https://headscale.net/stable/) and NetBird/WireGuard are *alternative transport research*, not claimed drop-in Tailscale Operator compatibility.
- [NVIDIA Personal AI Router](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Personal-AI-Router) / [downstream fork](https://github.com/kvnloo/Personal-AI-Router) — optional **model-serving request routing**, not GPU resource scheduler; [PAIR #85](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Personal-AI-Router/issues/85), [#91](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Personal-AI-Router/issues/91), [#92](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Personal-AI-Router/issues/92) and [PR #10](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Personal-AI-Router/pull/10) track non-multicast VPN node discovery. [Fork PR #2](https://github.com/kvnloo/Personal-AI-Router/pull/2) proposed actual serving-node attribution but was closed unmerged, so prove receipts independently.
- [Kueue](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue), [KAI](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/KAI-Scheduler), [KEDA](https://github.com/kedacore/keda) remain admission / GPU placement / elastic scaling owners. Existing z0/Evolution Lab/Tokenomics/z0evals provide only policy research and verified performance evidence; no autonomous routing/driver/platform changes.

### 5. Attention / next-action contract

**ACTIVE NOW:** validate current draft #46 on a disposable K3s host: exact-head CI, immutable image, PVC/environment identity across real Pod restart, authenticated private HTTPS/ACL, client pairing and negative controls (**NOT RUN** until executed). Then isolate/provision **one** P1 worker and prove existing T3 peer-delegation lifecycle. Next prove exclusive GPU scheduling *only when necessary and explicitly approved*. **WAIT:** Tailscale multi-cluster, PAIR engine routing, GPU fractioning, r620 compute fractions, and ABAB autonomous advice are future lanes with independent acceptance; they must not preempt the live P0/P1 blocker or manufacture separate work queues. Do not open duplicate upstream/fork issues or PRs for design-only references. Promotion queue [#42](https://github.com/kvnloo/t3code/issues/42) receives verified exact-head outcomes only.

items.title: spike(runtime): per-conversation persistent sessions with bounded execution and burst coalescing
items.body:
<!-- spike-planning-2026-10-23 -->
## Planning refresh — 2026-10-23

**Priority / disposition: P1 / DISCOVERY NEXT.**

No DevLoop execution found at audit time. Evaluate isolated per-conversation logical sessions, bounded compute, per-session serialization and burst coalescing. Start with fixtures and an architecture decision; preserve the existing Claude Remote operator session. Coordinate shared current-state research with #757 without merging their decisions.

Full audited inventory and Claude day plan: https://github.com/mctlhq/.github/issues/215

This is a planning disposition; workflow/proposal state and required approvals remain independently authoritative.
<!-- /spike-planning-2026-10-23 -->

## Context

MCTL already has most of the ingredients for a persistent proactive agent runtime:

- `mctl-claude-remote` keeps a long-lived operator-facing Claude session and can resume it across restarts;
- `mctl-events` can inject external events into a running Claude Channels session and requires explicit `ack_event` handling;
- `mctl-telegram` already models one agent-visible dialog as a `Conversation`, uniquely keyed by `(user_id, peer_tg_id)`;
- Telegram incoming messages are already durable, policy-governed, and tied to per-conversation state;
- Temporal is the existing durable orchestration substrate for agent workflows.

A long-standing MCTL idea is to give each Telegram chat its own isolated persistent agent context so history and working state from one chat never bleed into another. The key distinction is:

> **session-per-chat must not mean process-per-chat.**

MCTL may have hundreds of logical sessions while allowing only a small bounded pool of active Claude executions (for example 5). Inactive sessions remain durable/cold and resume only when a relevant event arrives.

This spike is intentionally separate from `mctl-agents#757`.

- `#757` asks whether MCTL needs a general Duet-style attention-routing/session contract across proactive agents.
- **This spike** asks whether a per-conversation isolated session model is practical and how it should compose with the existing Claude Remote operator session, Temporal, Telegram conversations, and execution limits.

## Core hypothesis

For Telegram and similar conversational sources, MCTL should be able to provide:

```text
Telegram account
  ├─ conversation A -> logical agent session A -> history/context A
  ├─ conversation B -> logical agent session B -> history/context B
  └─ conversation C -> logical agent session C -> history/context C
```

with:

- strict session/context isolation;
- durable identity/history across restarts;
- at most one active execution per logical session;
- a global bounded execution pool;
- cold resume instead of one permanently running process per chat;
- burst coalescing so several near-consecutive messages become one Claude turn/event where appropriate.

## Required relationship to existing Claude Remote

The spike must explicitly preserve two different but connected planes:

### 1. Operator plane — existing `mctl-claude-remote`

The current Claude Remote persistent session remains the human/operator session:

- interactive control/debugging;
- global operator context;
- current Channels/event integrations;
- no requirement that user conversation histories are injected into this transcript.

### 2. Conversation plane — per-chat logical sessions

Each external conversation gets an isolated logical agent session addressed by a stable MCTL identity, e.g.:

```text
telegram:<user_id>:<peer_tg_id>
```

These sessions may be implemented using Claude session resume, bounded workers, Temporal state, or a hybrid, but must **not** rely on the operator Claude Remote transcript as canonical conversation memory.

The spike must answer whether these per-chat sessions:

- reuse the same Claude Remote runtime/image with different session IDs;
- run through a dedicated worker/runtime using the same underlying Claude tooling;
- or use a hybrid where Claude Remote remains operator-only while conversation execution is separately managed.

Do not assume two independent orchestration systems. Temporal/MCTL must remain the authoritative execution coordinator if suitable.

## Questions to answer

### Q1. Session identity and storage

Determine the minimum session record and mapping from current Telegram `Conversation`:

```text
(user_id, peer_tg_id)
    -> conversation_id
    -> agent_session_id
```

Evaluate what must persist across cold resumes:

- Claude session/resume identifier, if used;
- bounded transcript/history or summary reference;
- current goals/state;
- last processed event/message cursor;
- pending actions/approvals;
- model/runtime version binding;
- timestamps/lifecycle state.

Do not store chain-of-thought or copy credentials into session state.

### Q2. Isolation boundary

Prove that session A cannot accidentally hydrate or mutate session B.

Evaluate isolation at all relevant layers:

- session identity;
- history/transcript;
- event routing;
- tool/API scope;
- approval/action binding;
- storage queries;
- encryption scope.

Today message content is tenant/user-key encrypted. Determine whether per-conversation derived encryption keys materially improve isolation and whether they are worth the operational complexity.

### Q3. Bounded execution pool

Model a runtime with many logical sessions and few active execution slots.

Starting experiment target:

```text
100 logical sessions
5 max concurrent Claude executions
1 max active execution per session
```

Required behavior:

```text
10 chats receive work
-> first 5 acquire execution slots
-> remaining 5 stay queued/durable
-> completed execution releases a slot
-> next waiting session resumes
```

Determine where concurrency belongs:

- Temporal worker concurrency;
- MCTL runtime semaphore/capacity manager;
- provider quota-aware scheduler;
- or a combination.

The limit must be configurable rather than hard-coded to 5.

### Q4. Per-session serialization

For one conversation, concurrent messages must not create competing Claude executions against the same history.

Required invariant:

```text
max_concurrent_per_session = 1
```

If an execution is active, new messages are queued/coalesced for the same session rather than starting another execution.

Prove race safety for:

- two events arriving at the same time;
- retry/redelivery;
- worker crash after work starts;
- session resume after restart.

### Q5. Message burst coalescing

This is a first-class requirement, not an optional optimization.

Users often send several short messages in sequence:

```text
"Hi"
"one more thing"
"here is the link"
```

Starting Claude once per message wastes tokens and gives worse context.

Evaluate a bounded debounce/coalescing policy:

```text
first message arrives
-> open short coalescing window
-> append additional messages from same conversation
-> emit one logical wake/event/turn
-> start/resume Claude once
```

The spike must determine:

- appropriate configurable quiet window / max wait;
- max messages / bytes per batch;
- behavior when the session is already executing;
- edits/deletes during the window;
- urgent/system events that must bypass coalescing;
- ordering and provenance of every original message;
- dedupe on Telegram event/message identity;
- whether deterministic filtering can suppress a model invocation entirely.

Measure LLM invocations and latency with coalescing enabled vs disabled.

### Q6. Cold resume and lifecycle

A logical session must not imply a permanently running process.

Evaluate:

```text
ACTIVE -> IDLE -> COLD -> RESUME -> ACTIVE
```

Questions:

- after how much idle time can compute be released?
- what exact state is required to resume safely?
- how expensive/slow is Claude session resume?
- when should a long session rotate to a fresh session with bounded summary/context?
- how does this compose with existing `mctl-claude-remote` transcript rotation behavior?

### Q7. Temporal architecture

Compare at least these shapes:

1. one long-lived Temporal workflow per conversation;
2. durable session record + short-lived Temporal executions;
3. one workflow per account with child/session coordination;
4. hybrid session coordinator + execution child workflows.

Compare:

- history growth / Continue-As-New;
- signal fan-in;
- worker concurrency;
- queue fairness;
- cancellation;
- retry/recovery;
- deployment/versioning;
- operational complexity;
- cost.

Do not introduce a second workflow engine.

### Q8. Queue fairness and quotas

Bounded execution introduces scheduling policy.

Evaluate at minimum:

- FIFO baseline;
- per-user/account fairness;
- `max_concurrent_per_user`;
- global `max_concurrent_executions`;
- protection from one noisy chat/account starving others;
- provider quota/rate-limit backpressure;
- priority for explicit owner/user interaction over background work if appropriate.

### Q9. Relationship to attention routing (`#757`)

Keep responsibilities separate:

- **this spike:** isolation, session identity, execution capacity, cold resume, message coalescing;
- **#757:** whether an event should be ignored, handled, notify the owner, or require approval.

Expected composition:

```text
incoming events/messages
-> conversation/session routing
-> deterministic dedupe + burst coalescing
-> attention decision (where applicable)
-> bounded execution admission
-> resume isolated session
-> governed tools/actions
```

### Q10. Generalization beyond Telegram

Telegram is the first bounded E2E experiment, but define whether the session key can generalize cleanly to other resources:

```text
telegram:<account>:<chat>
slack:<workspace>:<channel>:<thread>
github:<repo>:pr:<number>
```

Do not build generic multi-provider support in the spike; only ensure the session identity model does not unnecessarily hard-code Telegram semantics.

## Required bounded experiment

Build/prototype enough to prove the model with Telegram-like fixtures or a safe test account.

### Experiment A — isolation

```text
chat A -> session A
chat B -> session B
```

Prove:

- A and B have independent session identities/history;
- A's tools cannot fetch B's conversation through the scoped execution context;
- events for A never wake B;
- approval/action records remain bound to the correct conversation/session.

### Experiment B — bounded concurrency

Create 10 runnable sessions with runtime concurrency set to 5.

Prove:

- no more than 5 active executions at once;
- all 10 eventually process;
- one session never has >1 active execution;
- waiting work survives worker/runtime restart.

### Experiment C — burst coalescing

For one session, inject 3 messages inside the configured short window.

Expected:

```text
3 durable source messages
-> 1 coalesced logical wake/turn
-> 1 Claude invocation
-> ordered provenance preserved
```

Then inject a message after the quiet window and prove it creates a new wake.

### Experiment D — cold resume

Run one conversation, release compute, then deliver another message later.

Prove:

- same logical session is resumed;
- prior conversation context required for the reply is available;
- unrelated conversation context is absent;
- restart/crash does not lose the queued event or corrupt session mapping.

## Measurements

Record at minimum:

- active process/worker count for 10/100 logical sessions;
- memory/CPU while sessions are cold vs active;
- queue wait time at concurrency 5;
- resume latency;
- model invocations per N Telegram messages with and without burst coalescing;
- token/cost delta from coalescing;
- Temporal history growth by session/workflow model;
- storage size per logical session;
- failure/retry behavior;
- cross-session isolation test results;
- implementation footprint by repository.

## Invariants

1. **Session-per-chat is not process-per-chat.**
2. **At most one active execution per logical session.**
3. **Global execution concurrency is bounded and configurable.**
4. **Queued work is durable.** Waiting for a slot must survive process restart.
5. **Cross-session data access fails closed.**
6. **Burst coalescing never loses source-message provenance/order.**
7. **Coalescing is bounded.** A noisy sender cannot delay processing indefinitely.
8. **Provider/tool side effects still use existing policy/approval paths.**
9. **The operator Claude Remote transcript is not canonical per-chat memory.**
10. **Persistent logical state, ephemeral compute.**
11. **No second workflow engine.**
12. **No production rollout in the spike.**

## Deliverables

### D1. Current-state map

Map the exact roles of `mctl-telegram`, `mctl-claude-remote`, `mctl-events`, `mctl-agents`, Temporal, policy/approval, and conversation storage.

### D2. Session model

Define stable identity, lifecycle, persisted fields, and boundaries between operator and conversation sessions.

### D3. Runtime/concurrency decision

Recommend where global/per-user/per-session concurrency is enforced and how queued work is admitted fairly.

### D4. Burst coalescing contract

Define debounce/window, limits, provenance, urgent bypass, edits/deletes, and behavior while a session is active.

### D5. Isolation decision

Define tool/API scoping and whether per-conversation encryption is justified.

### D6. Temporal topology decision

Choose exactly one preferred workflow/session shape and document versioning/history/recovery consequences.

### D7. Bounded prototype evidence

Provide the results of experiments A-D and measurements.

### D8. Integration boundary with `mctl-claude-remote`

State explicitly whether per-chat executions reuse the Claude Remote image/runtime, share only common packaging, or are a separate execution service. Preserve the current operator persistent session either way.

### D9. Follow-up ownership map

For each proven gap:

`Gap | Repo | Existing issue | Extend/create | Priority | Dependency`

### D10. Final recommendation

Exactly one:

- `REUSE_CURRENT_RUNTIME_WITH_SESSION_ROUTER`
- `ADD_SHARED_CONVERSATION_SESSION_RUNTIME`
- `TEMPORAL_ONLY_COMPOSITION`
- `DO_NOT_IMPLEMENT_SESSION_PER_CONVERSATION`

## Non-goals

- replacing the existing operator Claude Remote session;
- one pod/process per Telegram chat;
- production rollout;
- implementing all of `#757` attention routing;
- building a generic message bus;
- building a generic multi-provider session product;
- bypassing policy/approval;
- storing chain-of-thought;
- unbounded transcript retention.

## Expected default hypothesis

> MCTL can preserve one isolated persistent logical session per conversation while running only a small, configurable pool of Claude executions. Telegram messages should be durably routed by conversation, short bursts coalesced before model invocation, and inactive sessions resumed cold on demand. The existing Claude Remote session remains the operator plane rather than becoming canonical storage for every external conversation.

Refs: `mctl-agents#757`, `mctl-telegram` communication agent, `mctl-claude-remote`/`mctl-events`.

items.title: perf(runner): maintain a capacity-scaled blank sandbox warm pool
items.body:
Parent: #24203

## Summary

Maintain a small Runner-owned pool of pristine, already-booted blank sandboxes for compatible cold
runs. Size the pool from effective Runner capacity, keep foreground admission authoritative, and
allow sufficiently old exact-idle inventory to yield capacity when exact entries would otherwise
prevent the blank pool from reaching its target.

PR #31970 implements the complete Runner-local lifecycle, including 30-minute oldest-first
exact-idle capacity yield.

## Evidence

The rolling production window recorded on #24203 showed cold creation as the remaining slow path:
approximately 7% of successful starts, with roughly 2.4 seconds p90. This window mixes frequent
Runner releases and is descriptive rather than a causal version comparison.

A read-only sample of the current `v0.186.8` processes on `prod-11`, `prod-12`, and `prod-13`
avoided that version mixing. From approximately 08:50 to 13:02 UTC on 2026-09-06:

- 812 accepted park-to-next-exact-reuse pairs had 0.39-second p50, 1.08-second p75,
  2.4-minute p90, and 9.3-minute p95;
- 57 pairs (7.0%) reached five minutes, 40 (4.9%) reached ten minutes, 13 (1.6%) reached
  thirty minutes, and 3 (0.4%) reached one hour;
- contemporaneous heartbeats reported 66 reusable exact sandboxes across the three hosts; and
- event reconstruction produced 68 approximate current entries, including 22 at least thirty
  minutes old and 14 at least one hour old. The two-entry difference is consistent with collection
  races and incomplete lifecycle pairing.

The sample supports 30 minutes as a conservative initial capacity-yield threshold: few observed
successful reuses crossed that age, while approximately one third of current exact inventory had.
It does not establish a globally optimal TTL, so the implementation remains conditional and
observable rather than introducing adaptive prediction.

For the observed `prod-11` profile shape, effective capacity is approximately 62 sandboxes and the
dynamic blank target is six. With active plus exact-idle occupancy near that capacity, free-capacity
refill alone can keep at most one blank despite a target of six.

## Required behavior

### Capacity-scaled blank pool

- Select the configured profile with the greatest effective fit capacity, with a stable profile-name tie-break.
- Calculate capacity from effective vCPU, effective memory, and any non-zero concurrent-job cap.
- Use a zero target below capacity two; otherwise target the nearest 10%, bounded below total capacity and by a non-zero `max_idle`.
- Keep enough CPU and memory headroom for the largest configured profile during ordinary refill.
- Use the existing one-second blank-pool tick and lifecycle wakeups; do not add a separate GC loop.

### Conditional exact-idle capacity yield

- Attempt ordinary immediate-only resource and background pre-spawn admission first.
- Consider retirement only when blank inventory is below target and ordinary refill is blocked by resource capacity, reserved headroom, or `max_idle`.
- Select only the oldest compatible exact entry whose Runner-local monotonic `parked_at` age is at least 30 minutes.
- Convert one entry at a time: remove it, publish status and request an immediate heartbeat, complete normal workspace promotion and physical destruction, then transfer its retained same-shape budget lease to one newly created blank.
- Recompute after each parked blank and use the existing one-second tick as fallback.
- Never reclassify an exact sandbox in place.
- Let a real pre-spawn waiter cancel background creation immediately; safely finish destruction already in progress and do not select another exact entry.

### Selection, safety, and compatibility

- Exact compatible reuse and possible workspace-cache reuse remain ahead of blank claims.
- When asynchronous activation rolls back an exact reservation, restore it ahead of a blank that filled its idle slot; preserve its original parked age and complete physical cleanup of the displaced blank.
- Reserve a compatible blank before foreground pressure eviction so a full Runner can still use its warm inventory; after provider claim, recheck exact inventory and authoritative workspace-cache metadata before activating that blank.
- Preserve `noReuseKey` attribution when candidate metadata advertises reuse but the authoritative claimed context does not.
- Under foreground pressure, consume or retire blank inventory before unrelated exact inventory.
- Blank preparation uses only profile/global device shape and an unseeded mounted workspace drive.
- Preserve typed sandbox, factory, and budget ownership through removal, promotion, physical cleanup, cancellation, panic, drain, and shutdown.
- Keep the behavior Runner-local with no API, database, queue, guest-wire, heartbeat-schema, status-schema, or persisted protocol change.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Dynamic target handles effective resources, concurrency caps, small capacities, capacity 62, and `max_idle` deterministically.
- [x] Ordinary preparation is single-flight, immediate-only, foreground-preemptible, and preserves largest-profile headroom.
- [x] Exact and workspace-cache reuse retain priority; blank claims retain existing miss attribution, including authoritative `noReuseKey`, and claim-time tenant setup.
- [x] Full-capacity foreground admission reserves compatible blank inventory before pressure eviction and rechecks exact and workspace-cache priority after provider claim.
- [x] Blank entries retain explicit ownership through activation, rollback, pressure, replacement, failure, cancellation, panic, drain, and shutdown.
- [x] A capacity- or `max_idle`-blocked deficit converts only the oldest compatible exact entry at or above the inclusive 30-minute boundary.
- [x] Conversion publishes revisioned idle status and heartbeat state before cleanup, uses normal workspace promotion/destruction, retains the same-shape budget lease through cleanup, and creates a new blank instead of reclassifying tenant state.
- [x] Conversion is one-at-a-time, recomputes after each parked blank, falls back to the existing one-second tick, and yields pre-spawn admission immediately to foreground work.
- [x] Low-cardinality telemetry distinguishes ordinary suppression, missing age eligibility, age-based retirement, cleanup failure/cancellation, and replacement completion.
- [x] Deterministic tests cover the threshold, compatibility, oldest-first and simultaneous eligibility, single-flight conversion, status/heartbeat refresh, resource exhaustion, `max_idle`, foreground interruption, authoritative post-claim reuse attribution, and uncertain cleanup; the full Runner suite covers the reused promotion, drain, shutdown, and ownership paths.
- [x] Current implementation passes Runner formatting, Clippy with warnings denied, rustdoc with warnings denied, and the full Runner suite (3,484 passed, 25 existing ignored; guest inventory passed).
- [x] Re-review the current head after the full-capacity admission, authoritative-attribution, and exact-reservation rollback fixes.
- [x] Complete current-head CI after the rollback-priority fix. The base mounted-blank lifecycle has same-build metal coverage; the aging path uses injected monotonic park times locally to avoid a wall-clock 30-minute test.

## Current status

- PR #31970 head `579d06a483` implements the 30-minute oldest-first capacity-yield path, preserves compatible blank admission at full Runner capacity, and keeps authoritative post-claim reuse attribution.
- Self-review additionally reproduced and fixed premature exact eviction when a blank filled the idle slot during asynchronous finalizing activation; cancellation rollback now restores the exact sandbox and cleans up the blank.
- Local Rust validation and repeated complete six-pass self-review are green on this head. Current-head CI is complete: 62 successful checks, 22 conditionally skipped checks, 0 pending, and 0 failed.
- Keep 30 minutes as the initial conservative policy and use post-deployment telemetry for any later tuning issue; do not add adaptive TTL logic here.

## Scope boundaries

- Do not preinstall tenant storage or maintain content-hash allowlists.
- Do not discard a valid workspace-cache hit.
- Do not fill all free capacity, batch-retire exact sandboxes, or add adaptive demand prediction.
- Do not change team concurrency, durable queue semantics, claim ordering, billing, authorization, or the real process-spawn boundary.

## Relevant code

- `crates/runner/src/resource_budget.rs`
- `crates/runner/src/idle_pool.rs`
- `crates/runner/src/idle_pool/`
- `crates/runner/src/cmd/start/blank_pool.rs`
- `crates/runner/src/cmd/start/idle_lifecycle.rs`
- `crates/runner/src/cmd/start/mod.rs`
- `crates/runner/src/executor/sandbox_run.rs`
- `crates/sandbox/src/sandbox.rs`
- `crates/sandbox-fc/src/sandbox.rs`

items.title: [Epic][Security] Red-team Connex — offensive source review fleet (gpt-6-astra xhigh)
items.body:
## Purpose

Adversarial, source-level red-team of Connex at `origin/main` **78cd6752d** (2026-09-12). Independent Codex lanes (`gpt-6-astra`, reasoning `xhigh`, read-only sandbox, no network, no builds) each own one attack surface and try to break it. Every lane report is logged on this issue as a comment; the ledger below is the triaged roll-up.

This epic is a **findings log**, not a fix tracker. Confirmed findings get their own child issues linked from the ledger; this issue closes when every lane has reported and every finding is either filed, rejected with a reason, or marked as a known issue.

## Tracking

- Linear project (Security team): https://linear.app/connexcrm/project/connex-red-team-offensive-source-review-sept-2026-fe6ea7f6708f — Security-team view of the engagement. Confirmed findings are filed as GitHub child issues; Linear issue creation is currently refused (free issue limit), so mirror them there once it allows.

## Threat model used

Attackers considered by every lane: (a) unauthenticated internet user; (b) authenticated member of tenant A attacking tenant B; (c) low-privilege member escalating inside a tenant; (d) hostile content (records, imports, uploads, inbound mail, AI prompt injection); (e) compromised third party (webhook sender, OAuth/SSO provider, delivery provider); (f) operator misconfiguration / deployment drift. Reference docs: `docs/THREAT_MODEL.md`, `docs/SECURITY.md`, `docs/backend/SECURITY_BOUNDARIES.md`, `docs/backend/LOCKING.md`, `docs/MULTITENANCY_PLAN.md`.

## Lanes

| # | Lane | Surface |
|---|------|---------|
| 01 | auth-session | AuthController/AuthService, session epoch + absolute timeout, fixation, logout, password reset, email change, registration verification, rate limits, privileged-MFA filter |
| 02 | webauthn-passkey | `webauthn/`, challenge binding, RP ID/origin, counters, passkey promotion, recovery tokens |
| 03 | sso-social-jit | `sso/`, SSO connections/links, social login, OIDC state/nonce, JIT provisioning, domain allowlists, account-link takeover |
| 04 | tenancy-routing | `tenant/`, resolution + scope interceptors, workspace cookie, catalog routing, unscoped mappers, EXEMPT/SCOPED namespaces |
| 05 | rbac-sharing-owner | permissions, roles, shares, owner/member scope, `@RequirePermission`, teams, role-edit escalation |
| 06 | idor-records | Person/Company/Deal/Note/Task/Activity/Tag/CustomField/SavedView/Segment/Search/GuidedRecordCreation — foreign ids in bodies, bulk ops |
| 07 | uploads-storage-ocr | attachments, quarantine, UploadContentInspector, object storage, business-card OCR client, image decode bounds |
| 08 | ai-masking-egress | `ai/` masking/demasking, prompt injection via record data, provider config secrets, budgets, STOMP streaming, assistant skills/tools that mutate |
| 09 | secrets-crypto | `secrets/`, encryption at rest, key rotation, API credentials, connector/delivery/mail configs, audit-integrity HMAC, diagnostics leakage |
| 10 | public-api-webhooks | `publicapi/`, v1 controllers, PublicApiSecurityConfig, PAT auth, delivery + signature webhooks, CSP report, unsubscribe, replay |
| 11 | csrf-cors-headers-ws | SecurityConfig, header-only CSRF handler, response headers, WebSocket/STOMP security, CORS, cookie flags, cache headers |
| 12 | injection-sql-mybatis | 121 mapper XMLs — `${}` interpolation, dynamic ORDER BY/columns, LIKE escaping, JSON paths, segment predicate builders, CSV/formula injection |
| 13 | frontend-xss-proxy | `proxy.ts` route protection, rewrites, `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, model-authored markdown rendering, open redirects, `NEXT_PUBLIC_`, public pages, CSP |
| 14 | data-lifecycle-dsr-export | DSR, exports, export grants, tenant lifecycle/teardown, support bundles, APPI incidents, retention |
| 15 | workflows-rules-automation | workflows/rules/sequences/schedules, action privilege, template injection, egress from actions, confused deputy, manual runs |
| 16 | campaigns-mail-delivery | campaigns, delivery providers, mail, unsubscribe/suppression tokens, SMTP SSRF, header/template injection, engagement tracking |

| 19 | deploy-supply-chain | `deploy/`, workflows, Caddyfile, compose, CI secrets, release signing, backups, maintenance mode, metrics token, actuator |
| 20 | org-admin-invites-membership | organizations, members, invites/invite links, allowed domains, teams, users, offboarding, last-admin lockout |
| 21 | notifications-comments-mentions | notifications, record comments, mentions across workspaces, STOMP user-queue subscriptions |

## Findings ledger

| 20 | F4 Custom role on sole owner strands the workspace | Medium | filed 1688 | verified: assignCustomRole bypasses last-owner guard |

## Method notes

- Lane prompt: shared preamble + per-lane charter. Lanes cite `path:line`, give concrete reproduction steps, and mark duplicates of open `Security` issues as known.
- Orchestrator triage: dedupe across lanes, reproduce or reason through each High+ finding against the source, reject false positives with a reason.
- No code was changed by this epic. Fixes belong in child issues.

---

## Engagement complete — executive summary (2026-09-13)

All **22 lanes reported** against `origin/main` 78cd6752d. Every finding above the evidence threshold was reproduced against source by the orchestrator before filing; duplicates across lanes were merged and each is noted as an independent confirmation.

**48 new child issues filed** (#1640–#1688), plus **14 existing open issues** annotated with new detail or independent corroboration. Distinct filed findings by severity: **4 Critical** (one rated Critical/High), **12 High**, **29 Medium**, **3 Low**. Several findings were reported by two independent lanes; those are counted once and marked as confirmations.

### Themes that recur across lanes
- **Credential-to-destination binding is missing in several places.** Changing an SMTP host (#1656) or OIDC issuer (#1657) with a blank secret forwards the stored secret to the new destination; email and SMS providers share one secret slot (#1655). Two lanes independently found the SMTP and shared-slot cases.
- **Realtime (STOMP) identity and lifecycle.** Queues are addressed by mutable username, so a recycled name leaks another tenant's notifications/AI to an old socket (#1661); sockets keep receiving after session revocation/logout (#1662). Both found by two lanes.
- **Authorization snapshotted before locks.** Share grants (#1652), contact restriction changes (#1685), and workflow enable (#1669) act on a permission read taken before contention, so a committed revocation doesn't stop the in-flight write. `requireRole` also ignores custom-role overlays (#1650).
- **Identity/verification trust.** Workspace-scoped authority mints globally-verified accounts (#1641); a preregistered unverified account intercepts an email invitation (#1687); enterprise SSO JIT takes over a passwordless social account cross-tenant (#1645).
- **Path-representation mismatch.** Security filters match the raw request URI while Spring routes the decoded path, bypassing export MFA step-up and the absolute-session timeout (#1643, found by two lanes).

### Reassuring negatives (no exploit found in the inspected paths)
- No SQL injection across all 121 mappers; every `${}` traces to a literal or a closed server-side registry (lane 12).
- No exploitable XSS, open redirect, or proxy/RSC auth bypass in the frontend paths reviewed (lane 13).
- All 130 tenant-data tables carry lifecycle declarations; no cross-tenant export or teardown authorization bypass (lane 14).
- Published images use digests, external Actions are pinned to SHAs, and the release pipeline verifies signatures (lane 19).
- Body-size, upload, OCR, and async-work limits are present across most paths (lane 22).

### Caveats
- Read-only source review: no builds, tests, or network. Runtime-dependent items — chiefly the encoded-path routing (#1643) and the multi-instance items — need confirmation against the deployed Caddy+Tomcat edge.
- Findings are inputs, not verdicts. Each child issue carries a concrete reproduction and a verification outline; owners should reproduce before and after the fix.

items.title: Configurable data classification (ISO 27001 / TISAX / BSI / TLP) replacing GDPR/NDA flags
items.body:
## Summary

Replace the two fixed compliance flags (GDPR / NDA) and the one-bit "confidential" conversation mark with a **configurable data classification**, as ISO/IEC 27001, TISAX, BSI IT-Grundschutz and TLP describe it. An operator defines an ordered list of levels (e.g. Public < Internal < Confidential < Strictly confidential), data classes that map onto those levels, and detectors that recognise them. Every destination data can reach (model pools, tools, MCP servers, connectors) carries a **maximum level**. A conversation's level only rises automatically; what the conversation may reach follows from comparing the two.

A fresh installation has exactly one level, so nothing changes and nothing is visible until an administrator sets the classification up with a guided assistant.

Scope: **person chats**. Agents, `/v1` request headers and #186 §3 (per-message egress guard for agents) build on this mechanism later.

Design walkthrough (flows, setup assistant, simulator): https://claude.ai/artifact/M6Cyi34sX2sEcRi4SUSWJQ

## Background: what the standards ask for

This is product guidance, not legal advice. AIplane enforces the operator's policy; the operator decides the classification and declares what each provider arrangement covers.

- **ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A.** A.5.12 classification, A.5.13 labelling (outputs included), A.5.14 information transfer, A.8.12 data leakage prevention, A.8.15 logging. The standard prescribes **no fixed levels**, so the scheme must be fully configurable (3–5 levels are typical).
- **Schemes to ship as templates.** ISO-typical (4 levels), TISAX / VDA ISA (public, internal, confidential, strictly confidential), BSI protection requirement (normal, high, very high), TLP 2.0 (CLEAR, GREEN, AMBER, AMBER+STRICT, RED).
- **GDPR.**
  - Art. 4(1), 9 and 10 define data *classes* (personal, special category, criminal).
  - Art. 25 asks for privacy by default.
  - Art. 28 and 44–49 (DPA, third-country transfer) are what a pool's maximum level declares.
  - Art. 5(2) and 30 require a content-free audit of every level change.
- **German trade secrets act, GeschGehG § 2 Nr. 1 b.** A secret is only protected under "appropriate confidentiality measures". Classification plus technical enforcement is such a measure; this is the main case for NDA material.
- **§ 203 StGB.** Professional secrecy (medical, legal, tax) is a data class with a high minimum level.

## Current state (what this replaces)

| Today | Where | Becomes |
|---|---|---|
| Pool flags `compliance_gdpr` / `compliance_nda` | `aiplane-core` `upstreams/config.rs` (`Compliance`), `db/upstreams_config.rs`, `db_bridge.rs` | one **maximum level** per pool |
| Sticky `confidential` bit | `chat_session_settings.confidential` (migration 0087), `POST …/confidential`, check in `openai_driver.rs` | the conversation's **level** |
| `chat.confidential.default` / `.requires` | `config.rs` `ConfidentialConfig`, `settings.rs` | default level of new conversations / gone |
| Content guard with two fixed System One questions, `gdpr_action` / `nda_action` | `aiplane-runtime/src/content_guard.rs` | System One detector: one question per data class, an action per class |
| `ToolPromptKind::ContentGuard` confirmation | `content_guard::confirm_in_chat` | reused for detector confirmation |
| GDPR/NDA badges in the model picker and pool editor | SPA (`#lib/model-option`, upstream editor) | one level chip |

Gaps the current design leaves, which this closes:

- Tools with outbound reach (`search_web`, `fetch_url`, MCP tools, image generation) ignore the mark.
- `session_share` makes any conversation readable by every signed-in user.
- Uploads are not classified before a model sees them.
- Generated files carry no marking.

## Concepts

- **Level.** One ordered list with a rank, a name, a description, a badge colour, an optional visible marking text, an optional Microsoft Purview label id, and a filename tag.
- **Data class.** What a detector recognises, e.g. "personal data", "health data", "customer under NDA". Each class points at one level. Only the level is enforced; the class is the reason recorded in the audit.
- **Conversation level.** `new = max(old, level of whatever entered)`. Raising is always automatic. Lowering is a policy setting: `never` or `by the user with a reason`. A lowering is audited.
- **Maximum level of a destination.** One value per model pool, tool, MCP server (covers its tools) and connector, set like a group grant. When the conversation's level exceeds it:
  - **Models** are hidden from the picker, and the turn is refused server-side.
  - **Tools** are either hidden or **gated**; this is set per destination. The gate is described below.
- **Source level.** A knowledge collection carries a level; a retrieval hit from it raises the conversation.

## Detectors

1. **Digital markings.** Always on, no configuration beyond mapping a found value to a level.
   - **Microsoft Purview / MIP.**
     - OOXML `docProps/custom.xml` `MSIP_Label_<GUID>_Enabled/_Name/_SiteId`, plus the newer `docMetadata/LabelInfo.xml`.
     - PDF XMP packet (`MSIP_Label_…`).
     - E-mail header `msip_labels`.
     - The mapping is keyed by label GUID, with the name as a fallback.
   - **TSCP / BAILS** custom properties (`urn:bails:…`, LibreOffice classification) in ODF and OOXML.
   - **E-mail `Sensitivity:`** header (RFC 2156: Personal, Private, Company-Confidential).
   - **Visible stamps** in the first part of a document's text: `VERTRAULICH`, `STRENG VERTRAULICH`, `CONFIDENTIAL`, `STRICTLY CONFIDENTIAL`, `INTERNAL USE ONLY`, `TLP:AMBER`/`TLP:RED`/…, `VS-NUR FÜR DEN DIENSTGEBRAUCH`. The patterns are pre-filled and editable.
   - **Classification tag in the filename** (the same pattern the output marking writes, see below).
   - **Fallback levels:**
     - A label value that is not mapped yet sets the configurable *unknown-label level* and is audited as "unmapped".
     - Encrypted or unreadable files set the configurable *unreadable level*.
     - When several markings disagree, the highest wins.
2. **Patterns with validation.** These run locally, never call out, and need no configuration beyond turning them on for a class:
   - e-mail address
   - IBAN (mod-97)
   - payment card number (Luhn)
   - German tax id (check digit)
3. **Word lists.** The administrator uploads a TXT file (one term per line) or a CSV file (they pick the column) for a data class.
   - The preview shows the term count and duplicates, and flags very short terms.
   - A re-upload replaces the list.
   - Matching is local, case-insensitive and on word boundaries.
   - Lists are visible to administrators only, never sent to a model, and audited (who, when, how many terms).
4. **System One rule** per data class: a question, one positive and one negative example, a threshold and an action (`raise` / `confirm` / `block`).
   - This generalises today's content guard.
   - **The System One model used for detection and for the gate must itself be cleared for the highest level.** The setup assistant refuses a model that is not; today it only warns.

Detection runs on:
- the user's message,
- **uploads at submit time, before any model sees them** (markings on the bytes, patterns, word lists and System One on the extracted text),
- retrieval hits (the collection's level).

## Tool gate

A tool whose maximum level is below the conversation's level and whose mode is `gate` stays available. Only its *arguments* leave AIplane, not the conversation. Before each call:

1. If the conversation's level is at or below the tool's maximum level, the call runs.
2. Otherwise the arguments are checked with patterns, word lists and System One, against the classes above the tool's level.
3. Clean arguments run the call.
4. A match either **asks the user** (approve or deny, the decision audited) or **blocks**, as configured. The ask reuses the approval protocol of `AskFirst` / `ask_first::approval` (`chat_turn_suspensions`).
5. If the gate model is unreachable, the call is blocked.

The check runs per call, so a level raised mid-turn (an attachment fetched, a retrieval hit) applies to the turn's next call.

## Output marking

A generated file gets the conversation's level at the time it was generated. Marking happens at **one place**: one helper that every generated-file upload goes through, used instead of the direct `chat_attachments::upload` calls in `aiplane-tools`, the sandbox and the MCP spill. An architecture test keeps it that way.

What is configured:
- per level: the visible text, the MIP label id and the filename tag,
- per format: visible marking, metadata and filename tag, each on or off.

| Output | Visible | Metadata | v1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| docx, xlsx, pptx | header/footer where feasible | `MSIP_Label_*` custom properties and TSCP | metadata yes; visible marking if it fits the round |
| odt, ods, odp | — | TSCP | yes |
| Markdown, TXT, HTML | banner line | HTML `<meta>` | yes |
| CSV, JSON, code | — | — (would break the format) | filename only: `offer-confidential.json` |
| Every format | — | — | filename tag `{name}-{tag}.{ext}`, replacing an existing tag rather than stacking |
| MIP labels with encryption | — | — | no: protection needs the MIP SDK in the tenant; AIplane labels only |

A generated file that is uploaded again is recognised by the marking reader, which closes the loop.

## Sharing and forks

- Sharing is internal only (signed-in users).
- **Link share** (today's `shared` flag) is allowed up to the configured *link-share maximum level*.
- Above that level, *Share* opens a picker of **users and groups**. Only those, plus the owner, can open the conversation.
- A fork inherits the source's level. It starts unshared, as today, and its sharing follows the same rules.

## Policy settings

These live in the admin settings rows (`settings.rs`); no new settings mechanism:

- default level for new conversations
- lowering: `never` | `by the user with a reason`
- gate on a match: `ask` | `block`
- link-share maximum level
- unknown-label level and unreadable level
- System One model used for detection and the gate
- mode: `monitor` (log what would happen; nothing is raised, hidden or blocked) | `enforce`

## Defaults and migration

- **New installations: one level, "Public".** Every destination is at that level. The UI shows no badge, no level selector and no share picker, and no gate and no output marking ever apply. The feature is active exactly when the scheme has more than one level.
- **Existing installations that use the old mechanism** (any pool with a GDPR or NDA flag off, the content guard enabled, or any conversation marked confidential) are migrated into a prepared ISO-typical scheme (Public < Internal < Confidential < Strictly confidential), with classes "personal data" → Internal and "NDA" → Confidential:
  - GDPR on, NDA on → highest level. This is the old "all-clear" default, so nothing changes for most installations.
  - GDPR on, NDA off → Internal.
  - GDPR off → Public. A single ordered axis cannot express "NDA but no DPA". The migration rounds down and records this in the migration log.
  - Confidential conversations → Confidential.
  - Content guard questions and actions → the System One rules of the two classes.
- **All other installations** get the one-level default.
- There is one migration for the whole change, amended in place while unpushed, with a schema fixture and a lossless-upgrade test.

## Setup assistant (admin)

A stepper under `/admin/classification` that produces a proposal; the administrator reviews it and applies it. This reuses the proposal → review → apply shape of the existing setup flows.

1. **Choose a path:** a template (ISO-typical, TISAX, BSI, TLP) or a custom scheme.
2. **Levels:** order, name, colour, description, default level.
3. **Data classes:** level, detectors, System One rule with examples, and a **test with a sample file** (shows what would be detected).
4. **Markings:** upload an already-labelled sample document. The assistant reads its label GUIDs and names and maps them to levels, suggesting a match by name.
5. **Destinations:** walk through every model pool, tool, MCP server and connector with progress per kind. For pools it asks where they run, whether a DPA is in place, the third-country basis and whether there is an NDA, and proposes a level. A destination left unrated gets the lowest level on activation, and the assistant lists those first.
6. **Output marking:** per-level text and label id, per-format switches.
7. **Policy:** lowering, gate, link-share maximum.
8. **Monitor run, then enforce.**

After activation the same page edits the configuration directly.

## Chat UI

- A level badge in the conversation header, showing the cause of the last raise ("Attachment Contract.docx: MIP label Confidential").
- A level selector in the composer. It replaces the Confidential checkbox, only raises, and can lower only if the policy allows it, with a reason.
- The model picker lists only cleared models.
- Gated tool calls show the existing approval prompt with the matched classes (never the matched text beyond what the user typed).
- The share dialog follows the link-share rules above.

## Audit

`chat_label_events` records, per conversation:
- from level, to level,
- the cause (`user`, `marking:<kind>`, `pattern:<id>`, `wordlist:<class>`, `system_one:<class>`, `source:<collection>`, `migration`),
- the actor and the reason.

Gate decisions are logged the same way. No content is stored. An admin view lists events with filters.

## Architecture (crate stack)

- `aiplane-core`: level/class types, tables and accessors, destination levels, the pool's maximum level in the upstream registry, policy settings.
- `aiplane-features` (new `classification/` module, no `AppState`): marking readers (OOXML, ODF, PDF XMP, e-mail, stamps, filename), patterns, word-list matching, output stamping.
- `aiplane-runtime`: System One detector (from `content_guard.rs`), conversation ratchet, tool filter (next to the grant narrowing in `openai_driver.rs`), tool gate, model filter.
- `aiplane-api`: `/api/v0/admin/classification/*`, chat level/share endpoints. `gateway` routes them.
- `session-core` stays owner-agnostic: it may store per-conversation user shares, but never groups or levels.

No new Cargo dependencies: `zip`, `quick-xml`, `mail-parser`, `pdfium-render` and `regex` are already in the workspace.

## Tests (required)

**Unit tests** for every reader, pattern validator, word-list matcher, the ratchet, the gate decision and the stamping per format.

**Integration tests** (`crates/aiplane/tests/it/`, wiremock upstreams, S3 mock), each run against **three schemes**:

- **Fresh installation (one level).**
  - All models and tools are available.
  - The chat API reports no level UI.
  - Uploads of labelled files change nothing.
  - Link share works as today.
- **ISO-typical 4-level scheme** and **BSI 3-level scheme**, each with a cleared and an uncleared pool and a gated `search_web`:
  - Upload a **`.docx` with an embedded MIP label** (`docProps/custom.xml`). The conversation is raised to the mapped level, the uncleared model disappears from the picker, and a turn naming it is refused.
  - Upload a **second labelled file of a different kind**: a PDF with an XMP MIP label, and an `.eml` with `Sensitivity: Company-Confidential`. Each raises the conversation to its mapped level.
  - Upload a file whose text carries a visible stamp (`TLP:AMBER`), and one whose label is unmapped, which falls back to the unknown-label level.
  - Lowering is refused under `never` and audited under `by the user with a reason`.
  - Gate on `search_web`: clean arguments pass; arguments with a word-list term ask (`ask`) or are refused (`block`). An unreachable gate model blocks.
  - Above the link-share maximum, link sharing is refused and a user share grants read access. A fork keeps the level.
  - A generated `.docx` and a generated `.json` carry the label and the filename tag, and uploading them again raises a fresh conversation to that level.
- **Migration test:** an installation with GDPR/NDA flags, the guard and confidential conversations upgrades losslessly into the mapped scheme; an untouched installation gets one level.

**Browser check of the UI by the coordinator:** setup assistant end to end, the badge, the picker, the gate prompt and the share picker.

## Documentation (same change)

- A new `docs/classification.md` (design + operator guide).
- Rewrite the GDPR/NDA parts of `docs/admin/models.md`, `docs/admin/settings.md`, `docs/admin/settings-reference.md`, `docs/upstreams.md` and `docs/ui.md`.
- Update the user guide on the chat badge and sharing, `docs/tools-inventory.md` where a tool's behaviour changes, and the docs index.
- All user-visible strings go through the six Fluent catalogs.

## Out of scope (follow-ups)

- Agents (a fixed maximum level from the agent spec; content above it refused), and #186 §3.
- `/v1` classification request header and response header.
- Applying protecting (encrypting) MIP labels.

items.title: Remote Firestore: extension-scoped sync client for sealed documents (browser and native)
items.body:
Part of #2463.

## Outcome

An extension (first Colab, #2452) can read, subscribe to and publish its already-sealed documents through a public, extension-scoped Remote client on a Firebase remote, from the browser and from the owner's machine, under the extension's declared Rules, without building its own Firebase transport and without any Admin or Rules bypass.

## Why this ticket exists

The first Firestore release is layer 1 (page sharing). Remote ships the Rules composer, the deploy, the hosted entry and the public link, but no client: the browser transport is #2506 (shaped around the SDK operations and object channel) and nothing offers a native connector. Colab #2452 therefore has no relay to sync through (core-1 audit, Colab lead ruling: Colab will not build its own transport). The cloud edge admission and machine connector of #2160 are layer 2 (device operations) and stay On Hold; this ticket is not that.

## Scope to plan (plan first, one bounded topic)

- The public extension-facing surface: bounded read, subscribe and publish of sealed documents under the extension's declared collections; verified project, extension and space; typed refusals reusing Remote's vocabulary; no operations authority; one charged target per commit (the accounting model of #2453 stays Colab's).
- Browser: how it relates to #2506 (one Firebase client, sign-in, public-config bootstrap and admission vocabulary shared; #2506 stays the browser sign-in and transport slice).
- Native: how the owner's machine reaches Firestore (a Firestore listen has no stable REST form, so compare a helper process, bounded polling and others), sign-in as an ordinary Firebase Auth user under the same Rules, credential storage in the owner home with owner-only permissions, explicit revoke and expiry, and who owns the serve lifecycle that calls it.
- Free-plan cost: reads, writes and Rules lookups per operation feed the guard model (#2691).

## Acceptance (to be refined by the plan)

Emulator-level proof of sign-in, a permitted read, subscribe and write, a refused write and a typed refusal on loss of access, from both the browser and the native client; the contract defines the surface once; Colab, Core and UX confirm their parts; no claim beyond what ships.

## Dependencies and authorization

Authorization (owner, 2026-10-11): the Firestore hold is lifted and model quota is green; plan and development proceed. The native credential's type, storage and lifecycle are decided by the Remote lead within the owner's principles: an owner-only file or the OS keychain (macOS first), defaults modeled on comparable tools (gh, firebase-tools, gcloud, docker credential helpers, cloud SSO sessions), every default adjustable through Remote settings (storage method, lifetime/expiry, refresh behaviour; the settings UI is epic #2738), least disruptive first with stricter modes opt-in, default refresh and expiry. The plan records the decision and the comparison; only a real security concern that breaks these principles goes back to the owner. Real-account proof stays in #2166 (held; separate exact authorization). Order: contract and plan, then browser (#2506), then native. Staffing: remote-1 plans under my review.

Squad: tmt-remote. Primary: tmt-remote-lead. Plan-first; Todo and not started.
